questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating age-group proportions to classify age pyramids as expanding, stable or declining, and calculating per capita birth and death rates
questions.question:
Three populations have the following percentages of individuals:

Population | Pre-reproductive | Reproductive | Post-reproductive
P | 45 | 40 | 15
Q | 30 | 40 | 30
R | 15 | 45 | 40

A fourth population of 1500 individuals had 180 births and 75 deaths in a year. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) P is declining, Q expanding, R stable; birth rate 180 per year
B) All three are stable because the reproductive group is 40–45 % in each
C) P is stable and R expanding; birth rate 0.05 and death rate 0.12 per individual per year

D) P (large pre-reproductive base) is expanding with a triangular pyramid, Q (similar young and old groups) is stable with a bell-shaped pyramid, and R (small young group) is declining with an urn-shaped pyramid; the per capita birth rate is 180/1500 = 0.12 and death rate 75/1500 = 0.05 per individual per year, giving a net increase of 105 individuals (7 %)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P expanding, Q stable, R declining; birth rate 0.12, death rate 0.05 per individual per year.
Concept: A population has certain attributes that an individual organism does not; an individual may have births and deaths, but a population has birth rates and death rates; in a population these rates refer to per capita births and deaths, respectively; the rates, hence, are expressed as change in numbers (increase or decrease) with respect to members of the population; for example, if in a pond there were 20 lotus plants last year and through reproduction 8 new plants are added, taking the current population to 28, we calculate the birth rate as 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus per year. Another attribute characteristic of a population is sex ratio. A population at any given time is composed of individuals of different ages; if the age distribution (per cent individuals of a given age or age group) is plotted for the population, the resulting structure is called an age pyramid; for human population, the age pyramids generally show age distribution of males and females in a combined diagram; the shape of the pyramids reflects the growth status of the population — whether (a) it is growing (expanding, triangular with a broad base), (b) stable (bell-shaped) or (c) declining (urn-shaped, with a narrow base).
Given: Age percentages for P, Q, R; N = 1500, births 180, deaths 75.
Formula/Principle: Birth rate = births/N; death rate = deaths/N; pyramid shape from the size of the pre-reproductive group relative to the others.
Step 1: P: 45 % young > reproductive > old ⇒ expanding (triangle).
Step 2: Q: young ≈ old ⇒ stable (bell); R: young smallest ⇒ declining (urn).
Step 3: b = 180/1500 = 0.12; d = 75/1500 = 0.05; net +105.
Why: The pre-reproductive group forms the future breeding population, so its size relative to the others predicts growth.
Why not the others: (A) Labels mixed; birth rate must be per capita. (B) Shapes differ because the young and old groups differ. (C) Labels and rates swapped.
Key point: Triangular = expanding, bell = stable, urn = declining; rates are per capita.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of steps in decomposition of detritus, the products formed, and the factors that speed or slow decomposition
questions.question: Which sequence and description of decomposition is correct?
options: A) Mineralisation → humification → fragmentation → leaching; decomposition is fastest in cold, dry soil

B) Detritivores such as earthworms break detritus into smaller particles (fragmentation) → water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and precipitate as unavailable salts (leaching) → bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances (catabolism) → a dark, amorphous, colloidal substance, humus, accumulates, which is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes very slowly (humification) → humus is further degraded by some microbes to release inorganic nutrients (mineralisation); decomposition is faster when detritus is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars, and in warm, moist conditions, and slower when it is rich in lignin and chitin, at low temperature or under anaerobiosis
C) Humus decomposes very fast and is the first product of decomposition
D) Decomposition is an anaerobic process that does not need oxygen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation; rate depends on chemical composition and climate.
Concept: Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients, and the process is called decomposition. Dead plant remains such as leaves, bark, flowers and dead remains of animals, including fecal matter, constitute detritus, which is the raw material for decomposition. The important steps in the process of decomposition are fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation. Detritivores (e.g. earthworm) break down detritus into smaller particles; this process is called fragmentation. By the process of leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts. Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances; this process is called catabolism; it is important to note that all the above steps in decomposition operate simultaneously on the detritus. Humification and mineralisation occur during decomposition in the soil; humification leads to accumulation of a dark coloured amorphous substance called humus that is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate; being colloidal in nature it serves as a reservoir of nutrients; the humus is further degraded by some microbes and release of inorganic nutrients occurs by the process known as mineralisation. Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process; the rate of decomposition is controlled by chemical composition of detritus and climatic factors; in a particular climatic condition, the decomposition rate is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker if detritus is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars; temperature and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors that regulate decomposition through their effects on the activities of soil microbes; warm and moist environment favour decomposition whereas low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition, resulting in build up of organic materials.
Step 1: Fragmentation by detritivores; leaching of soluble nutrients.
Step 2: Catabolism by microbial enzymes.
Step 3: Humification (humus) followed by mineralisation.
Why: Breaking detritus into fragments increases the surface for microbial enzymes, and nutrients are finally returned to the soil as inorganic ions.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed; cold, dry conditions slow decomposition. (C) Humus is resistant and decomposes slowly. (D) Decomposition is largely aerobic.
Key point: Fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation; lignin/chitin and cold slow it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the four major causes of biodiversity loss (the 'Evil Quartet') with examples, and why co-extinctions occur
questions.question: Which explanation of the causes of biodiversity loss is correct?
options: A) Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause, as when tropical rain forests, once covering 14 per cent of the land surface, now cover no more than 6 per cent, and when large habitats are broken into fragments that cannot support animals needing large territories; over-exploitation drove the Steller's sea cow and passenger pigeon to extinction; alien species become invasive, as Parthenium, Lantana and water hyacinth, or the African catfish Clarias gariepinus threatening native catfishes; and co-extinctions occur because when a species becomes extinct, plant and animal species associated with it obligatorily (such as parasites of a host fish or a plant and its specific pollinator) also become extinct
B) Biodiversity is lost only because of natural disasters, and human activity plays no part
C) Introduced species always increase biodiversity because they add new species
D) Over-exploitation affects only plants, and co-extinction means two unrelated species dying at the same time by chance
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasions and co-extinctions, with examples.
Concept: The colonisation of tropical Pacific Islands by humans is said to have led to the extinction of more than 2,000 species of native birds; the IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species (including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years. The accelerated rates of species extinctions that the world is facing now are largely due to human activities; there are four major causes ('The Evil Quartet' is the sobriquet used to describe them). Habitat loss and fragmentation: this is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction; the most dramatic examples of habitat loss come from tropical rain forests; once covering more than 14 per cent of the earth's land surface, these rain forests now cover no more than 6 per cent; when large habitats are broken up into small fragments due to various human activities, mammals and birds requiring large territories and certain animals with migratory habits are badly affected, leading to population declines. Over-exploitation: humans have always depended on nature for food and shelter, but when 'need' turns to 'greed', it leads to over-exploitation of natural resources; many species extinctions in the last 500 years (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon) were due to overexploitation by humans. Alien species invasions: when alien species are introduced unintentionally or deliberately for whatever purpose, some of them turn invasive, and cause decline or extinction of indigenous species; invasive weed species like carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) pose a threat to native species; the recent illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture purposes is posing a threat to the indigenous catfishes in our rivers. Co-extinctions: when a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct; when a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets the same fate; another example is the case of a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism where extinction of one invariably leads to the extinction of the other.
Why: Species depend on suitable habitat, sustainable harvesting, freedom from new competitors and predators, and on the partners they are tied to; removing any of these drives extinctions.
Why not the others: (B) Current extinction rates are largely due to human activities. (C) Invasive aliens cause decline of native species. (D) Over-exploitation affects animals too; co-extinction involves obligate associates.
Key point: Evil Quartet: habitat loss, over-exploitation, alien invasions, co-extinctions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting organisms in each of Whittaker's five kingdoms and counting those with cell walls, using the criteria of cell structure, body organisation, nutrition and reproduction
questions.question: Classify bacterium, Nostoc, Amoeba, Chlamydomonas, yeast, mushroom, moss and earthworm in Whittaker's five-kingdom system. How many fall in Monera, Protista and Fungi, and how many of the eight have a cell wall?
options: A) Monera 1, Protista 3, Fungi 1; cell wall 5
B) Monera 2, Protista 1, Fungi 3; cell wall 8

C) Monera 2 (bacterium, Nostoc), Protista 2 (Amoeba, Chlamydomonas), Fungi 2 (yeast, mushroom); 6 have a cell wall (all except Amoeba and earthworm); the criteria are cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships
D) Monera 2, Protista 2, Fungi 2; cell wall 4, since fungi have no walls
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Monera 2, Protista 2, Fungi 2; 6 with a cell wall.
Concept: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed a five kingdom classification; the kingdoms defined by him were named Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia; the main criteria for classification used by him include cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. Monera includes prokaryotes (bacteria and cyanobacteria such as Nostoc and Anabaena), with a non-cellulosic (polysaccharide + amino acid) cell wall. Protista includes unicellular eukaryotes; the five kingdom classification brought together Chlamydomonas and Chlorella (earlier placed in Algae within Plants and both having cell walls) with Paramoecium and Amoeba (which were earlier placed in the animal kingdom and lack cell walls); cell wall is present in some protists. Fungi are heterotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall made of chitin and polysaccharides, including unicellular yeast and multicellular mushrooms. Plantae (e.g. mosses) have a cellulose cell wall. Animalia (e.g. earthworm) lack a cell wall.
Given: Eight organisms.
Formula/Principle: Assign by cell type (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), cellularity, nutrition; tally cell walls.
Step 1: Prokaryotes: bacterium, Nostoc ⇒ Monera = 2.
Step 2: Unicellular eukaryotes: Amoeba, Chlamydomonas ⇒ Protista = 2; yeast, mushroom ⇒ Fungi = 2.
Step 3: Cell wall absent in Amoeba and earthworm ⇒ 8 − 2 = 6.
Why: Kingdom placement rests on several criteria together, so organisms with walls can still be grouped with wall-less ones in Protista.
Why not the others: (A) Nostoc is a moneran; Chlamydomonas and Amoeba alone are protists here; yeast and mushroom are fungi. (B) Chlamydomonas is a protist; not all have walls. (D) Fungi have chitin walls.
Key point: Five kingdoms by cell structure, body organisation, nutrition, reproduction, phylogeny.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Arranging Cyclostomata, Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes and Amphibia in the order in which key vertebrate features appear, with their distinguishing characters
questions.question: Which sequence and description is correct?
options: A) Amphibia → Osteichthyes → Chondrichthyes → Cyclostomata, as limbs appeared before jaws

B) Cyclostomata (jawless, circular sucking mouth, 6–15 pairs of gill slits, ectoparasites that migrate to fresh water to spawn and die after spawning) → Chondrichthyes (jaws, cartilaginous endoskeleton, placoid scales, ventral mouth, gill slits without an operculum, no air bladder so they must swim constantly to avoid sinking, internal fertilisation with claspers in males, many viviparous) → Osteichthyes (bony endoskeleton, operculum covering the gills, air bladder for buoyancy, cycloid or ctenoid scales, mostly external fertilisation and oviparous) → Amphibia (two pairs of limbs, moist scaleless skin, tympanum, lungs, three-chambered heart, cloaca, external fertilisation and indirect development)
C) Chondrichthyes have an air bladder and operculum, while bony fishes lack both
D) Amphibians have a four-chambered heart and dry scaly skin
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cyclostomata → Chondrichthyes → Osteichthyes → Amphibia, with features listed.
Concept: All living members of the class Cyclostomata are ectoparasites on some fishes; they have an elongated body bearing 6–15 pairs of gill slits for respiration; cyclostomes have a sucking and circular mouth without jaws; their body is devoid of scales and paired fins; cranium and vertebral column are cartilaginous; circulation is of closed type; cyclostomes are marine but migrate for spawning to fresh water; after spawning, within a few days, they die; their larvae, after metamorphosis, return to the ocean (e.g. Petromyzon, Myxine). Chondrichthyes are marine animals with streamlined body and have cartilaginous endoskeleton; mouth is located ventrally; notochord is persistent throughout life; gill slits are separate and without operculum (gill cover); the skin is tough, containing minute placoid scales; teeth are modified placoid scales which are backwardly directed; their jaws are very powerful; these animals are predaceous; due to the absence of air bladder, they have to swim constantly to avoid sinking; heart is two-chambered; sexes are separate; in males pelvic fins bear claspers; they have internal fertilisation and many of them are viviparous (e.g. Scoliodon, Pristis, Carcharodon, Trygon). Osteichthyes includes both marine and fresh water fishes with bony endoskeleton; their body is streamlined; mouth is mostly terminal; they have four pairs of gills which are covered by an operculum on each side; skin is covered with cycloid/ctenoid scales; air bladder is present which regulates buoyancy; heart is two-chambered; sexes are separate; fertilisation is usually external; they are mostly oviparous and development is direct. Amphibians can live in aquatic as well as terrestrial habitats; most of them have two pairs of limbs; body is divisible into head and trunk; the amphibian skin is moist (without scales); a tympanum represents the ear; alimentary canal, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a common chamber called cloaca which opens to the exterior; respiration is by gills, lungs and through skin; the heart is three-chambered (two auricles and one ventricle); these are cold-blooded animals; sexes are separate; fertilisation is external; they are oviparous and development is indirect.
Step 1: No jaws ⇒ Cyclostomata.
Step 2: Jaws with cartilage ⇒ Chondrichthyes; bone, operculum, air bladder ⇒ Osteichthyes.
Step 3: Limbs and lungs for life on land ⇒ Amphibia.
Why: Each step adds a feature — jaws, then bone and buoyancy control, then limbs and lungs — that opened new ways of life.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed. (C) Features of cartilaginous and bony fishes swapped. (D) Amphibians have a three-chambered heart and moist skin.
Key point: Jawless → cartilaginous jawed → bony with air bladder → tetrapod amphibian.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the functions of epidermal tissue system structures, what the ground tissue system includes, and the arrangement of vascular bundles in roots, stems and leaves
questions.question: Which explanation of plant tissue systems is correct?
options: A) The ground tissue system includes the epidermis and vascular bundles
B) Root hairs are multicellular and help prevent water loss, while trichomes absorb water
C) Monocot stems have open vascular bundles with cambium, and roots have conjoint bundles

D) The epidermal tissue system — epidermis, stomata and epidermal appendages — protects the plant; stomata regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange, each guard cell having a thin outer wall and a thick inner wall so that it bends to open the pore when turgid; root hairs are unicellular elongations that absorb water and minerals, while trichomes on stems are usually multicellular and help prevent water loss; all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles form the ground tissue (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, and mesophyll in leaves); vascular bundles with cambium are open (dicot stems), without cambium closed (monocots), radial in roots and conjoint in stems and leaves
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Epidermal structures and their functions; ground tissue composition; open/closed, radial/conjoint bundles.
Concept: On the basis of their structure and location, there are three types of tissue systems: the epidermal tissue system, the ground or fundamental tissue system and the vascular or conducting tissue system. The epidermal tissue system forms the outer-most covering of the whole plant body and comprises epidermal cells, stomata and the epidermal appendages — the trichomes and hairs. Stomata are structures present in the epidermis of leaves; stomata regulate the process of transpiration and gaseous exchange; each stoma is composed of two bean-shaped cells known as guard cells which enclose stomatal pores; in grasses, the guard cells are dumb-bell shaped; the outer walls of guard cells (away from the stomatal pore) are thin and the inner walls (towards the stomatal pore) are highly thickened. The root hairs are unicellular elongations of the epidermal cells and help absorb water and minerals from the soil; on the stem the epidermal hairs are called trichomes; the trichomes in the shoot system are usually multicellular; they may be branched or unbranched and soft or stiff; they may even be secretory; the trichomes help in preventing water loss due to transpiration. All tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles constitute the ground tissue; it consists of simple tissues such as parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma; in leaves, the ground tissue consists of thin-walled chloroplast-containing cells and is called mesophyll. In dicotyledonous stems, cambium is present between phloem and xylem; such vascular bundles, because of the presence of cambium, possess the ability to form secondary xylem and phloem tissues, and hence are called open vascular bundles; in the monocotyledons, the vascular bundles have no cambium present in them and hence are called closed. When xylem and phloem within a vascular bundle are arranged in an alternate manner along the different radii, the arrangement is called radial, such as in roots; in conjoint type of vascular bundles, the xylem and phloem are jointly situated along the same radius, which is common in stems and leaves.
Why: Each tissue system's structure suits its job — protection and exchange at the surface, support and storage in the ground tissue, conduction in the vascular bundles.
Why not the others: (A) Ground tissue excludes epidermis and vascular bundles. (B) Root hairs are unicellular and absorb; trichomes reduce water loss. (C) Monocot bundles are closed; roots have radial bundles.
Key point: Epidermal (protection, exchange), ground (all else), vascular (open/closed, radial/conjoint).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining differences between plant and animal cells — cell wall, central vacuole, plastids, centrioles and mode of cytokinesis — and their consequences
questions.question: Which explanation of differences between plant and animal cells is correct?
options: A) A plant cell placed in a hypotonic solution swells but does not burst because its rigid cell wall resists expansion, while an animal cell, lacking a wall, may burst; the large central vacuole keeps plant cells turgid; plastids such as chloroplasts are found in plant cells but not animal cells; centrioles are absent from cells of higher plants, which still form a spindle; and in cytokinesis animal cells form a furrow in the plasma membrane while plant cells, enclosed by a wall, form a cell plate that grows from the centre outwards
B) Animal cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, and plant cells lack vacuoles
C) Plant cells divide by furrowing because they have centrioles
D) Both cell types burst equally in hypotonic solutions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Cell wall prevents bursting; central vacuole maintains turgor; plastids in plants; no centrioles in higher plants; cell plate vs furrow.
Concept: Plant cells possess a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole which are absent in animal cells; on the other hand, animal cells have centrioles which are absent in almost all plant cells. The cell wall is a non-living rigid structure which forms an outer covering for the plasma membrane of fungi and plants; the cell wall not only gives shape to the cell and protects the cell from mechanical damage and infection, it also helps in cell-to-cell interaction and provides a barrier to undesirable macromolecules. The vacuole is the membrane-bound space found in the cytoplasm; it contains water, sap, excretory product and other materials not useful for the cell; the vacuole is bound by a single membrane called the tonoplast; in plant cells the vacuoles can occupy up to 90 per cent of the volume of the cell; water entering by osmosis pushes the protoplast against the wall, making the cell turgid. Plastids are found in all plant cells and in euglenoides; they bear specific pigments, thus imparting specific colours to the plants; based on the type of pigments, plastids can be classified into chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts. Cytokinesis in an animal cell is achieved by the appearance of a furrow in the plasma membrane; the furrow gradually deepens and ultimately joins in the centre, dividing the cell cytoplasm into two; plant cells, however, are enclosed by a relatively inextensible cell wall, therefore they undergo cytokinesis by a different mechanism; in plant cells, wall formation starts in the centre of the cell and grows outward to meet the existing lateral walls; the formation of the new cell wall begins with the formation of a simple precursor, called the cell-plate, that represents the middle lamella between the walls of two adjacent cells.
Why: The rigid wall is the key difference: it resists osmotic swelling and forces plant cells to divide by building a new wall from inside.
Why not the others: (B) Plant cells have cellulose walls and large vacuoles. (C) Plant cells form a cell plate and lack centrioles. (D) The wall protects plant cells from bursting.
Key point: Wall, central vacuole, plastids in plants; centrioles in animals; cell plate vs furrow.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the separation of tissue into acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions, and the distinction between primary and secondary metabolites, to an analysis of a plant extract
questions.question: A student grinds a plant tissue in trichloroacetic acid and filters it. The filtrate contains small molecules; the retentate contains large ones. The plant also yields morphine and codeine. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Lipids are found in the filtrate because their molecular weight is below 1000 Da
B) Morphine and codeine are primary metabolites essential for normal growth

C) The filtrate (acid-soluble pool) has compounds with molecular weights of about 18 to 800 Da — amino acids, sugars and nucleotides — while the retentate (acid-insoluble fraction) has proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides and also lipids, which, though under 800 Da, form membranes that break into insoluble vesicles on grinding; morphine and codeine are alkaloids, secondary metabolites, along with flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics and pigments, while water is the most abundant chemical in living organisms
D) The acid-insoluble fraction contains only proteins
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Acid-soluble: small molecules; acid-insoluble: macromolecules and lipids; morphine and codeine are secondary metabolites (alkaloids); water most abundant.
Concept: A living tissue is ground in trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH) using a mortar and a pestle to obtain a thick slurry; when strained through a cheesecloth or cotton, two fractions are obtained: the filtrate or, more technically, the acid-soluble pool, and the retentate or the acid-insoluble fraction; scientists have found thousands of organic compounds in the acid-soluble pool. Molecular weights of compounds in the acid-soluble pool range from 18 to around 800 daltons (Da) approximately; the acid-insoluble fraction has only four types of organic compounds, i.e. proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids; these classes of compounds, with the exception of lipids, have molecular weights in the range of ten thousand daltons and above; lipids, whose molecular weights do not exceed 800 Da, come under the acid-insoluble fraction because they are present not in isolated form but arranged into structures like cell membrane and other membranes; when we grind a tissue, we are disrupting the cell structure; cell membrane and other membranes are broken into pieces and form vesicles which are not water soluble. The acid-soluble pool represents roughly the cytoplasmic composition; water is the most abundant chemical in living organisms (70–90 per cent). In animal tissues, one notices the presence of all such categories of compounds, which are called primary metabolites; however, when one analyses plant, fungal and microbial cells, one would see thousands of compounds other than these primary metabolites, e.g. alkaloids, flavonoids, rubber, essential oils, antibiotics, coloured pigments, scents, gums and spices; these are called secondary metabolites; while primary metabolites have identifiable functions and play known roles in normal physiological processes, we do not at the moment understand the role or functions of all the secondary metabolites in host organisms; however, many of them are useful to human welfare (e.g. rubber, drugs, spices, scents and pigments); alkaloids include morphine and codeine, and drugs include vinblastine and curcumin.
Why: Separation depends on whether molecules are soluble in acid; lipids behave as part of membranes, not as small free molecules.
Why not the others: (A) Lipids appear in the acid-insoluble fraction. (B) Alkaloids are secondary metabolites. (D) It also contains nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids.
Key point: Acid-insoluble: proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides, lipids; alkaloids are secondary metabolites.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting peptide bonds and amino acids in a multi-chain protein, counting possible tripeptides, and identifying levels of protein structure
questions.question: Adult haemoglobin has two α chains of 141 amino acids and two β chains of 146 amino acids. How many amino acids and peptide bonds does it contain, how many different tripeptides can be made from the 20 amino acids, and which statement about protein structure is correct?
options: A) 287 amino acids, 286 peptide bonds; 60 tripeptides; haemoglobin has only primary structure
B) 574 amino acids, 573 peptide bonds; 8000 tripeptides; the α-helix is left-handed
C) 574 amino acids, 574 peptide bonds; 1140 tripeptides; quaternary structure means the sequence of amino acids

D) 574 amino acids and 570 peptide bonds (each chain of n residues has n − 1 bonds); 20³ = 8000 tripeptides; the primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, secondary structure includes the right-handed α-helix, tertiary structure is the three-dimensional folding of a chain, and haemoglobin's arrangement of four subunits is its quaternary structure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 574 amino acids; 570 peptide bonds; 8000 tripeptides; four levels of structure.
Concept: Proteins are polypeptides; they are linear chains of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; each protein is a polymer of amino acids; as there are 20 types of amino acids, a protein is a heteropolymer. The sequence of amino acids, i.e. the positional information in a protein — which is the first amino acid, which is second, and so on — is called the primary structure of a protein; a protein is imagined as a line, the left end represented by the first amino acid (N-terminal) and the right end by the last (C-terminal). A protein thread does not exist throughout as an extended rigid rod; the thread is folded in the form of a helix; in proteins, only right-handed helices are observed; other regions of the protein thread are folded into other forms in what is called the secondary structure; in addition, the long protein chain is also folded upon itself like a hollow woollen ball, giving rise to the tertiary structure, which gives us a 3-dimensional view of a protein; tertiary structure is absolutely necessary for the many biological activities of proteins. Some proteins are an assembly of more than one polypeptide or subunits; the manner in which these individual folded polypeptides or subunits are arranged with respect to each other is the architecture of a protein, otherwise called the quaternary structure; adult human haemoglobin consists of 4 subunits — two of these are identical to each other; hence, two subunits of α type and two subunits of β type together constitute the human haemoglobin (Hb).
Given: 2 × 141 + 2 × 146 residues; 20 amino acids.
Formula/Principle: Peptide bonds per chain = n − 1; number of sequences of length k = 20ᵏ.
Step 1: Amino acids = 282 + 292 = 574.
Step 2: Bonds = 2(140) + 2(145) = 570.
Step 3: Tripeptides = 20³ = 8000.
Why: Peptide bonds join residues within a chain only; the four chains of haemoglobin are held together by non-covalent interactions.
Why not the others: (A) Counts only one α and one β; 20 × 3 is not the count; Hb has all levels. (B) Treats Hb as one chain; helix is right-handed. (C) Bonds miscounted; quaternary means subunit arrangement.
Key point: Bonds = residues − chains; 20ᵏ sequences; quaternary = subunit assembly.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting bivalents, chromatids, DNA content and possible gamete combinations in meiosis I for an organism with 2n = 24, and the events of the substages of prophase I
questions.question: For an organism with 2n = 24 whose G₁ nucleus has 2C DNA, how many bivalents and chromatids are present at pachytene, what is the DNA content after meiosis I and in a gamete, and how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment alone produce?
options: A) 12 bivalents, 48 chromatids; 2C after meiosis I and C in a gamete; 2¹² = 4096; synapsis with a synaptonemal complex occurs in zygotene, crossing over (with recombinase and recombination nodules) in pachytene, chiasmata appear in diplotene, and terminalisation of chiasmata occurs in diakinesis
B) 24 bivalents, 24 chromatids; 4C after meiosis I; 24 gametes; crossing over occurs in leptotene
C) 12 bivalents, 24 chromatids; C after meiosis I; 2²⁴ gametes; synapsis occurs in diakinesis
D) 6 bivalents, 48 chromatids; 2C in a gamete; 144 gametes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 12 bivalents, 48 chromatids; 2C after meiosis I, C in gametes; 4096 combinations; substages of prophase I.
Concept: Meiosis involves two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division called meiosis I and meiosis II but only a single cycle of DNA replication; meiosis I is initiated after the parental chromosomes have replicated to produce identical sister chromatids at the S phase; meiosis involves pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes; four haploid cells are formed at the end of meiosis II. Prophase I is longer and more complex: during leptotene the chromosomes become gradually visible under the light microscope; zygotene: chromosomes start pairing together, and this process of association is called synapsis; such paired chromosomes are called homologous chromosomes; synapsis is accompanied by the formation of a complex structure called the synaptonemal complex; the complex formed by a pair of synapsed homologous chromosomes is called a bivalent or a tetrad; pachytene: bivalent chromosomes now clearly appear as tetrads; this stage is characterised by the appearance of recombination nodules, the sites at which crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of the homologous chromosomes; crossing over is also an enzyme-mediated process and the enzyme involved is called recombinase; diplotene is recognised by the dissolution of the synaptonemal complex and the tendency of the recombined homologous chromosomes of the bivalents to separate from each other except at the sites of crossovers; these X-shaped structures are called chiasmata; diakinesis is marked by terminalisation of chiasmata. In anaphase I the homologous chromosomes separate, while sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres; each daughter cell of meiosis I is haploid in chromosome number but its chromosomes are still double (two chromatids). Random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I allows 2ⁿ combinations, where n is the haploid number.
Given: 2n = 24; G₁ = 2C.
Formula/Principle: Bivalents = n; chromatids = 4 × bivalents; combinations = 2ⁿ.
Step 1: n = 12 ⇒ 12 bivalents, 48 chromatids (DNA 4C after S).
Step 2: After meiosis I: 4C/2 = 2C; after meiosis II: C.
Step 3: 2¹² = 4096 combinations.
Why: Each bivalent orients independently at metaphase I, and DNA is halved twice after replicating once.
Why not the others: (B) Bivalents equal n, not 2n; wrong stage for crossing over. (C) Chromatids are four per bivalent; synapsis is in zygotene. (D) n is 12; gametes are C.
Key point: n bivalents, 4n chromatids; 2ⁿ combinations; synapsis zygotene, crossing over pachytene.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining how a proton gradient builds up across the thylakoid membrane, how it drives ATP synthesis, and why cyclic photophosphorylation makes ATP but not NADPH
questions.question: Which explanation of chemiosmosis in chloroplasts is correct?
options: A) Protons accumulate in the stroma, and ATP is made as they move into the lumen
B) Chemiosmosis needs no membrane, since ATP synthase floats freely in the stroma

C) Protons accumulate in the lumen because water is split on the lumen side, releasing H⁺ there; because the primary electron acceptor on the outer side passes its electron to a hydrogen carrier, which removes a proton from the stroma and releases it into the lumen; and because NADP reductase on the stroma side uses H⁺ from the stroma to reduce NADP⁺; the resulting gradient drives H⁺ back to the stroma through the CF₀ channel of ATP synthase, and CF₁ makes ATP; in cyclic photophosphorylation electrons from PS I return to PS I, so ATP is made but NADP⁺ is not reduced
D) Cyclic photophosphorylation produces NADPH because PS II is involved
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Proton accumulation in lumen from water splitting, H carrier, NADP reductase; CF₀/CF₁ ATP synthesis; cyclic gives only ATP.
Concept: ATP synthesis is linked to development of a proton gradient across the membranes of the thylakoid; the protons accumulate inside the membrane of the thylakoid (in the lumen); this is because (a) since splitting of the water molecule takes place on the inner side of the membrane, the protons or hydrogen ions that are produced by the splitting of water accumulate within the lumen of the thylakoids; (b) as electrons move through the photosystems, protons are transported across the membrane; this happens because the primary acceptor of electrons, which is located towards the outer side of the membrane, transfers its electron not to an electron carrier but to an H carrier; hence, this molecule removes a proton from the stroma while transporting an electron; when this molecule passes on its electron to the electron carrier on the inner side of the membrane, the proton is released into the inner side or the lumen side of the membrane; (c) the NADP reductase enzyme is located on the stroma side of the membrane; along with electrons that come from the acceptor of electrons of PS I, protons are necessary for the reduction of NADP⁺ to NADPH + H⁺; these protons are also removed from the stroma; hence, within the chloroplast, protons in the stroma decrease in number, while in the lumen there is accumulation of protons. The ATP synthase enzyme consists of two parts: one called the CF₀ is embedded in the thylakoid membrane and forms a transmembrane channel that carries out facilitated diffusion of protons across the membrane; the other portion is called CF₁ and protrudes on the outer surface of the thylakoid membrane on the side that faces the stroma; the break down of the gradient provides enough energy to cause a conformational change in the CF₁ particle of the ATP synthase, which makes the enzyme synthesise several molecules of energy-packed ATP. Chemiosmosis requires a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase. When only PS I is functional, the electron is circulated within the photosystem and the phosphorylation occurs due to cyclic flow of electrons; this results only in the synthesis of ATP, but not of NADPH + H⁺.
Why: Three processes move or remove protons on opposite sides of the membrane, building a gradient whose energy ATP synthase captures.
Why not the others: (A) Gradient direction reversed. (B) A membrane is essential to hold the gradient. (D) Cyclic flow involves only PS I and makes no NADPH.
Key point: Lumen H⁺ high (water splitting, H carrier, NADP reductase); CF₀ channel, CF₁ makes ATP.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the path of electrons through complexes I–IV of the mitochondrial electron transport system, the role of oxygen and ATP synthase, ATP yields from NADH and FADH₂, and the effect of blocking complex IV
questions.question: Which explanation of the electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation is correct?
options: A) Oxygen is needed only in glycolysis, and blocking complex IV has no effect on ATP synthesis

B) Electrons from NADH enter at complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) and pass to ubiquinone, while those from FADH₂ enter through complex II (succinate dehydrogenase); reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) passes electrons to complex III (cytochrome bc₁), then via mobile cytochrome c to complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, with cytochromes a and a₃ and two copper centres), which passes them to oxygen to form water; the energy creates a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis by complex V (ATP synthase, F₀ as proton channel and F₁ as the catalytic headpiece); one NADH yields about 3 ATP and one FADH₂ about 2 ATP; a poison that blocks complex IV stops electron flow and ATP synthesis, showing that oxygen drives the whole process by acting as the final hydrogen acceptor
C) FADH₂ yields more ATP than NADH because it enters at complex I
D) Cytochrome c is a fixed protein inside complex III
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Complexes I → Q → III → cyt c → IV → O₂; complex II for FADH₂; ATP synthase F₀/F₁; 3 and 2 ATP; blocking IV stops ATP.
Concept: The metabolic pathway through which the electron passes from one carrier to another is called the electron transport system (ETS) and it is present in the inner mitochondrial membrane; electrons from NADH produced in the mitochondrial matrix during the citric acid cycle are oxidised by an NADH dehydrogenase (complex I), and electrons are then transferred to ubiquinone located within the inner membrane; ubiquinone also receives reducing equivalents via FADH₂ (complex II) that is generated during oxidation of succinate in the citric acid cycle; the reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) is then oxidised with the transfer of electrons to cytochrome c via cytochrome bc₁ complex (complex III); cytochrome c is a small protein attached to the outer surface of the inner membrane and acts as a mobile carrier for transfer of electrons between complex III and IV; complex IV refers to cytochrome c oxidase complex containing cytochromes a and a₃, and two copper centres. When the electrons pass from one carrier to another via complex I to IV in the electron transport chain, they are coupled to ATP synthase (complex V) for the production of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate; the number of ATP molecules synthesised depends on the nature of the electron donor; oxidation of one molecule of NADH gives rise to 3 molecules of ATP, while that of one molecule of FADH₂ produces 2 molecules of ATP; although the aerobic process of respiration takes place only in the presence of oxygen, the role of oxygen is limited to the terminal stage of the process; yet, the presence of oxygen is vital, since it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system; oxygen acts as the final hydrogen acceptor. Complex V consists of two major components, F₁ and F₀; the F₁ headpiece is a peripheral membrane protein complex and contains the site for synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate; F₀ is an integral membrane protein complex that forms the channel through which protons cross the inner membrane; the passage of protons through the channel is coupled to the catalytic site of the F₁ component for the production of ATP; for each ATP produced, 2H⁺ pass through F₀ from the intermembrane space to the matrix down the electrochemical proton gradient.
Why: Electron flow to oxygen is what pumps protons; stopping it at any point collapses the gradient and ATP synthesis stops.
Why not the others: (A) Oxygen is the final acceptor in the ETS. (C) FADH₂ enters later (complex II) and yields fewer ATP. (D) Cytochrome c is a mobile carrier.
Key point: I/II → Q → III → cyt c → IV → O₂; NADH 3 ATP, FADH₂ 2 ATP.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining chemical synaptic transmission, why it is one-way, and how electrical synapses differ
questions.question: Which explanation of synaptic transmission is correct?
options: A) At a chemical synapse, the arrival of an action potential at the axon terminal stimulates synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft; they bind specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, opening ion channels so that ions enter and a new potential develops, which may be excitatory or inhibitory; transmission is one-way because only the pre-synaptic terminal releases transmitter; at electrical synapses, the pre- and post-synaptic membranes are very close and current flows directly from one neuron to the next, so transmission is faster, but such synapses are rare in our system
B) Neurotransmitters are released from the post-synaptic membrane and travel back to the axon
C) Electrical synapses are slower than chemical synapses because they need transmitters
D) The synaptic cleft is absent at chemical synapses
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Vesicle release, receptor binding, new excitatory or inhibitory potential; one-way; electrical synapses faster and rare.
Concept: A nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another through junctions called synapses; a synapse is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the synaptic cleft; there are two types of synapses, namely electrical synapses and chemical synapses. At electrical synapses, the membranes of pre- and post-synaptic neurons are in very close proximity; electrical current can flow directly from one neuron into the other across these synapses; transmission of an impulse across electrical synapses is very similar to impulse conduction along a single axon; impulse transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster than that across a chemical synapse; electrical synapses are rare in our system. At a chemical synapse, the membranes of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons are separated by a fluid-filled space called the synaptic cleft; chemicals called neurotransmitters are involved in the transmission of impulses at these synapses; the axon terminals contain vesicles filled with these neurotransmitters; when an impulse (action potential) arrives at the axon terminal, it stimulates the movement of the synaptic vesicles towards the membrane where they fuse with the plasma membrane and release their neurotransmitters in the synaptic cleft; the released neurotransmitters bind to their specific receptors present on the post-synaptic membrane; this binding opens ion channels, allowing the entry of ions which can generate a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron; the new potential developed may be either excitatory or inhibitory.
Why: Transmitter is stored and released only on the pre-synaptic side, and receptors are only on the post-synaptic side, so signals pass one way.
Why not the others: (B) Release is pre-synaptic. (C) Electrical synapses are faster. (D) Chemical synapses have a cleft.
Key point: Chemical synapse: vesicles → transmitter → receptors → new potential; electrical synapse faster, rare.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence from non-disjunction in meiosis to the karyotypes and features of Down's, Klinefelter's and Turner's syndromes, and how polyploidy differs
questions.question: Which sequence and description of chromosomal disorders is correct?
options: A) A gene mutation in one chromosome causes all three syndromes, and polyploidy is common in humans
B) Down's syndrome has 45 chromosomes, Klinefelter's is XO and Turner's is XXY
C) Turner's syndrome individuals are fertile males with an extra Y chromosome

D) Failure of chromatids to segregate during cell division (non-disjunction) → a gamete gains or loses a chromosome → fertilisation gives an aneuploid zygote → trisomy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes) causes Down's syndrome, with short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, a broad palm with a characteristic crease and retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development; 47, XXY causes Klinefelter's syndrome (sterile males with overall masculine development but feminine features such as development of breasts, gynaecomastia); 45, XO causes Turner's syndrome (sterile females with rudimentary ovaries and lack of secondary sexual characters); failure of cytokinesis after telophase gives polyploidy, often seen in plants
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Non-disjunction → aneuploid gamete → aneuploid zygote; Down's (trisomy 21), Klinefelter's (XXY), Turner's (XO); polyploidy from failed cytokinesis.
Concept: The chromosomal disorders are caused due to absence or excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes; failure of segregation of chromatids during the cell division cycle results in the gain or loss of a chromosome(s), called aneuploidy; for example, Down's syndrome results from the gain of an extra copy of chromosome 21; similarly, Turner's syndrome results due to loss of an X chromosome in human females; failure of cytokinesis after the telophase stage of cell division results in an increase in a whole set of chromosomes in an organism, and this phenomenon is known as polyploidy; this condition is often seen in plants. The total number of chromosomes in a normal human cell is 46 (23 pairs); out of these, 22 pairs are autosomes and one pair is sex chromosomes; sometimes, though rarely, either an additional copy of a chromosome may be included in an individual or an individual may lack one of any one pair of chromosomes; these situations are known as trisomy or monosomy of a chromosome, respectively. Down's syndrome: the cause of this genetic disorder is the presence of an additional copy of chromosome number 21 (trisomy of 21); this disorder was first described by Langdon Down (1866); the affected individual is short statured with a small round head, furrowed tongue and partially open mouth; the palm is broad with a characteristic palm crease; physical, psychomotor and mental development is retarded. Klinefelter's syndrome: this genetic disorder is also caused due to the presence of an additional copy of the X chromosome, resulting in a karyotype of 47, XXY; such an individual has overall masculine development; however, feminine development (development of breast, i.e. gynaecomastia) is also expressed; such individuals are sterile. Turner's syndrome: such a disorder is caused due to the absence of one of the X chromosomes, i.e. 45 with XO; such females are sterile as ovaries are rudimentary, besides other features including lack of other secondary sexual characters.
Step 1: Non-disjunction at meiosis ⇒ n + 1 or n − 1 gamete.
Step 2: Fusion with a normal gamete ⇒ 2n + 1 or 2n − 1 zygote.
Step 3: Identify syndrome from the karyotype (47, +21; 47, XXY; 45, XO).
Why: An extra or missing chromosome changes the dosage of hundreds of genes, producing characteristic syndromes.
Why not the others: (A) These are numerical chromosomal changes, not gene mutations; polyploidy is common in plants. (B) Karyotypes swapped. (C) Turner's individuals are sterile females lacking an X.
Key point: Down 47, +21; Klinefelter 47, XXY; Turner 45, XO.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Applying the laws of dominance and segregation to a test cross, a cross with incomplete dominance, and a loss-of-function allele
questions.question: (i) A violet-flowered pea plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a white-flowered plant. (ii) Red and white snapdragons (Antirrhinum) are crossed and the F₁ selfed. (iii) A mutant allele codes for a non-functional enzyme, but heterozygotes look normal. Which prediction is correct?
options: A) (i) All offspring will always be violet; (ii) F₂ is 3 red : 1 white
B) (iii) The mutant allele is dominant because it is the changed one

C) (i) If the offspring are about 1 violet : 1 white, the plant is heterozygous (Vv), and if all are violet it is homozygous (VV) — this is a test cross; (ii) F₁ are pink and F₂ shows 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so the phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same (incomplete dominance); (iii) the mutant allele is recessive because the single normal allele makes enough functional enzyme to give the normal phenotype
D) (ii) F₂ shows 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 because two genes are involved
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Test cross reveals genotype; incomplete dominance gives 1 : 2 : 1; non-functional allele is recessive.
Concept: Mendel's law of dominance states that characters are controlled by discrete units called factors, factors occur in pairs, and in a dissimilar pair of factors one member of the pair dominates (dominant) the other (recessive); the law of segregation states that the two alleles of a pair segregate or separate during gamete formation such that a gamete receives only one of the two factors. In a typical monohybrid cross, one cannot tell whether a dominant-phenotype plant is homozygous or heterozygous; to determine the genotype, Mendel crossed it with the recessive parent, called a test cross; in a typical test cross an organism showing a dominant phenotype is crossed with the recessive parent; if all progeny show the dominant phenotype, the parent was homozygous, and a 1 : 1 ratio shows it was heterozygous. The inheritance of flower colour in the dog flower (snapdragon or Antirrhinum sp.) is a good example of incomplete dominance; in a cross between true-breeding red-flowered (RR) and true-breeding white-flowered plants (rr), the F₁ (Rr) was pink; when the F₁ was self-pollinated the F₂ resulted in the ratio 1 (RR) Red : 2 (Rr) Pink : 1 (rr) White; here the genotype ratios were exactly as we would expect in any Mendelian monohybrid cross, but the phenotype ratios had changed from the 3 : 1 dominant : recessive ratio. When a modified allele produces a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme at all, the phenotype may effectively depend only on the functioning of the unmodified allele; the unmodified (functioning) allele, which represents the original phenotype, is the dominant allele and the modified allele is generally the recessive allele.
Why: Segregation predicts gamete types, and whether the heterozygote matches a parent depends on how much product one functional allele makes.
Why not the others: (A) A heterozygote gives some white; snapdragon F₂ is 1 : 2 : 1. (B) A non-functional allele is usually recessive. (D) Only one gene is involved.
Key point: Test cross: 1 : 1 ⇒ heterozygous; incomplete dominance F₂ 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the evidence for the RNA world, why DNA replaced RNA as the genetic material, and the Central Dogma with its retroviral exception
questions.question: Which explanation of the RNA world hypothesis, the replacement of RNA by DNA as the genetic material, and the Central Dogma is correct?
options: A) DNA was the first genetic material because it is a catalyst, and RNA evolved from it later for stability

B) RNA was probably the first genetic material, since essential life processes such as metabolism, translation and splicing evolved around RNA, which can act both as genetic material and as a catalyst (ribozyme); but RNA is reactive and unstable — the 2′-OH group on each nucleotide makes it labile and easily degradable, and it mutates faster — so DNA, with deoxyribose, thymine in place of uracil and a complementary double strand that resists change and allows repair, evolved from RNA and became the stable store; information flows DNA → RNA → protein (Central Dogma), but in retroviruses it flows from RNA to DNA by reverse transcription
C) RNA is more stable than DNA because it is single-stranded
D) The Central Dogma states that proteins are copied back into RNA in all cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) RNA world; RNA catalytic but unstable; DNA evolved for stability; Central Dogma with reverse transcription in retroviruses.
Concept: RNA was the first genetic material; there is now enough evidence to suggest that essential life processes (such as metabolism, translation, splicing, etc.) evolved around RNA; RNA used to act as a genetic material as well as a catalyst (there are some important biochemical reactions in living systems that are catalysed by RNA catalysts and not by protein enzymes); but RNA being a catalyst was reactive and hence unstable; therefore, DNA has evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable; DNA being double stranded and having a complementary strand further resists changes by evolving a process of repair. The 2′-OH group present at every nucleotide in RNA is a reactive group and makes RNA labile and easily degradable; RNA is also now known to be catalytic, hence reactive; DNA is chemically less reactive and structurally more stable when compared to RNA; therefore, among the two nucleic acids, DNA is a better genetic material; in fact, the presence of thymine at the place of uracil also confers additional stability to DNA; both DNA and RNA are able to mutate; in fact, RNA, being unstable, mutates at a faster rate; consequently, viruses having an RNA genome and a shorter life span mutate and evolve faster. Francis Crick proposed the Central Dogma in molecular biology, which states that the genetic information flows from DNA → RNA → Protein; in some viruses the flow of information is in the reverse direction, that is, from RNA to DNA.
Why: A good catalyst must be reactive, but a good store of information must be stable, so the two roles shifted to RNA/proteins and DNA respectively.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed. (C) RNA is less stable. (D) Proteins are not copied into RNA; the reversal is RNA → DNA in retroviruses.
Key point: RNA world; DNA more stable (deoxyribose, thymine, double strand); DNA → RNA → protein.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the fraction of labelled progeny when a ³²P-labelled or ³⁵S-labelled bacteriophage infects bacteria in unlabelled medium, and the results of the Avery–MacLeod–McCarty enzyme experiment
questions.question: A single bacteriophage with both strands of its DNA labelled with ³²P infects a bacterium in unlabelled medium and produces 100 progeny phages. In a parallel experiment, a phage whose protein coat is labelled with ³⁵S infects a bacterium. How many progeny contain ³²P, how many contain ³⁵S, and which statement about the experiments establishing DNA as genetic material is correct?
options: A) 100 contain ³²P and 100 contain ³⁵S; Avery found that protease destroyed transformation
B) 50 contain ³²P; 50 contain ³⁵S; Hershey and Chase found radioactive protein inside bacteria
C) 1 contains ³²P; 1 contains ³⁵S; Griffith showed that DNA is the transforming principle

D) 2 contain ³²P (each original labelled strand ends up in one progeny DNA by semi-conservative replication) and none contains ³⁵S (the coat stays outside); Hershey and Chase found radioactivity in bacterial cells after infection with ³²P-phages but in the supernatant with ³⁵S-phages, and Avery, MacLeod and McCarty found that DNase destroyed the transforming principle while protease and RNase did not
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2 progeny with ³²P; 0 with ³⁵S; Hershey–Chase and Avery–MacLeod–McCarty results.
Concept: In 1928, Frederick Griffith, in a series of experiments with Streptococcus pneumoniae, witnessed a miraculous transformation in the bacteria: injecting a mixture of heat-killed S strain and live R strain killed mice, and he concluded that the R strain bacteria had somehow been transformed by the heat-killed S strain bacteria — some 'transforming principle', transferred from the heat-killed S strain, had enabled the R strain to synthesise a smooth polysaccharide coat; however, the biochemical nature of genetic material was not defined from his experiments. Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty (1933–44) worked to determine the biochemical nature of the 'transforming principle'; they discovered that protein-digesting enzymes (proteases) and RNA-digesting enzymes (RNases) did not affect transformation, so the transforming substance was not a protein or RNA; digestion with DNase did inhibit transformation, suggesting that the DNA caused the transformation. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952) grew some viruses on a medium that contained radioactive phosphorus and some others on a medium that contained radioactive sulfur; viruses grown in the presence of radioactive phosphorus contained radioactive DNA but not radioactive protein, because DNA contains phosphorus but protein does not; similarly, viruses grown on radioactive sulfur contained radioactive protein but not radioactive DNA, because DNA does not contain sulfur; radioactive phages were allowed to attach to E. coli bacteria; then, as the infection proceeded, the viral coats were removed from the bacteria by agitating them in a blender, and the virus particles were separated from the bacteria by spinning them in a centrifuge; bacteria which were infected with viruses that had radioactive DNA were radioactive, indicating that DNA was the material that passed from the virus to the bacteria; bacteria that were infected with viruses that had radioactive proteins were not radioactive; this indicates that proteins did not enter the bacteria from the viruses. DNA replicates semi-conservatively, so each parental strand ends up in a different daughter molecule.
Given: One phage with two ³²P strands; 100 progeny; ³⁵S only in coat protein.
Formula/Principle: Semi-conservative replication: each parental strand persists in one daughter duplex; coat protein does not enter the cell.
Step 1: Two labelled parental strands ⇒ at most 2 progeny DNA molecules carry ³²P.
Step 2: Remaining 98 progeny are made entirely from unlabelled precursors.
Step 3: ³⁵S coat stays outside ⇒ 0 labelled progeny.
Why: Only the material that enters the host and is passed on can appear in the next generation, and parental DNA strands are conserved individually.
Why not the others: (A) Labelled atoms are not multiplied; protease did not stop transformation. (B) Protein did not enter; strands are not shared by 50 progeny. (C) Two strands give two labelled progeny; Griffith did not identify DNA.
Key point: ³²P (DNA) enters, ³⁵S (protein) does not; parental strands go to 2 progeny.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the Oparin–Haldane idea of chemical evolution, the conditions on early Earth, the results of Miller's experiment, and how spontaneous generation was disproved
questions.question: Which explanation of the origin of life is correct?
options: A) Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g. RNA, protein), with the formation of life preceded by chemical evolution, i.e. formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents; early Earth had high temperature, volcanic storms and a reducing atmosphere containing CH₄, NH₃ and other gases; in 1953 S. L. Miller created similar conditions in a closed flask with CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800 °C and electric discharge and observed formation of amino acids; Louis Pasteur showed in pre-sterilised flasks that life comes only from pre-existing life, dismissing spontaneous generation; the first non-cellular forms of life could have originated about 3 billion years back
B) Life arose spontaneously from decaying matter, as Pasteur's experiments proved
C) The early atmosphere was rich in free oxygen, which was essential for amino acid synthesis in Miller's experiment
D) Miller's experiment produced complete living cells within a week
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane); reducing early atmosphere; Miller made amino acids; Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation.
Concept: The universe is very old, almost 20 billion years old; the earth was supposed to have been formed about 4.5 billion years back; there was no atmosphere on early earth; water vapour, methane, carbon dioxide and ammonia released from molten mass covered the surface; the UV rays from the sun broke up water into hydrogen and oxygen, and the lighter H₂ escaped; oxygen combined with ammonia and methane to form water, CO₂ and others; the ozone layer was formed; as it cooled, the water vapour fell as rain, to fill the depressions and form oceans; life appeared 500 million years after the formation of earth, i.e. almost four billion years back. Some scientists believe that it came from outer space; early Greek thinkers thought units of life called spores were transferred to different planets including earth; for a long time it was also believed that life came out of decaying and rotting matter like straw, mud, etc. — this was the theory of spontaneous generation; Louis Pasteur by careful experimentation demonstrated that life comes only from pre-existing life; he showed that in pre-sterilised flasks, life did not come from killed yeast while in another flask open to air, new living organisms arose from 'killed yeast'; spontaneous generation theory was dismissed once and for all. Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g. RNA, protein, etc.) and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution, i.e. formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents; the conditions on earth were high temperature, volcanic storms, and a reducing atmosphere containing CH₄, NH₃, etc.; in 1953, S.L. Miller, an American scientist, created similar conditions in a laboratory scale; he created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800 °C; he observed formation of amino acids; in similar experiments others observed formation of sugars, nitrogen bases, pigments and fats. The first non-cellular forms of life could have originated 3 billion years back; they would have been giant molecules (RNA, protein, polysaccharides, etc.); the first cellular forms of life did not originate till about 2000 million years ago.
Why: Energy from heat and lightning acting on reducing gases can produce the building blocks of life, which later assembled into self-replicating systems.
Why not the others: (B) Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation. (C) The early atmosphere was reducing. (D) Only organic molecules, not cells, were formed.
Key point: Chemical evolution in a reducing atmosphere; Miller made amino acids; life from pre-existing life (Pasteur).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting observations on primary and secondary immune responses, active and passive immunity, colostrum and antibody structure, and the barriers of innate immunity
questions.question: (i) A person receives a vaccine and, months later, meets the same pathogen; antibody levels rise much faster and higher than after the first exposure. (ii) A person bitten by a snake is injected with antibodies against the venom and is protected at once. (iii) A newborn fed colostrum resists infections in early months. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) (i) is passive immunity because the vaccine contains antibodies
B) (ii) is active immunity, giving long-lasting memory

C) (i) The first exposure produced a low-intensity primary response and memory B and T cells, so the second exposure gave an anamnestic secondary response (active immunity); (ii) ready-made antibodies give quick but short-lived passive immunity; (iii) colostrum contains abundant IgA antibodies that protect the infant (passive immunity); each antibody has four peptide chains, two small light and two longer heavy chains (H₂L₂), and classes include IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG; innate immunity includes physical, physiological, cellular (neutrophils, monocytes, natural killer lymphocytes, macrophages) and cytokine (interferon) barriers
D) Antibodies are made of two chains only, both identical heavy chains
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Secondary (anamnestic) response from memory; antivenom passive; colostrum IgA passive; H₂L₂ antibodies; innate barriers.
Concept: Innate immunity is a non-specific type of defence that is present at the time of birth; it is accomplished by providing different types of barriers to the entry of foreign agents into our body; innate immunity consists of four types of barriers: (i) physical barriers — skin on our body is the main barrier, and mucus coating of the epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts also helps in trapping microbes; (ii) physiological barriers — acid in the stomach, saliva in the mouth, tears from eyes all prevent microbial growth; (iii) cellular barriers — certain types of leukocytes (WBC) of our body like polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils) and monocytes and natural killer (type of lymphocytes) in the blood as well as macrophages in tissues can phagocytose and destroy microbes; (iv) cytokine barriers — virus-infected cells secrete proteins called interferons which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection. Acquired immunity is pathogen specific and characterised by memory; when our body encounters a pathogen for the first time it produces a response called primary response which is of low intensity; subsequent encounter with the same pathogen elicits a highly intensified secondary or anamnestic response; this is ascribed to the fact that our body appears to have memory of the first encounter. B-lymphocytes produce an army of proteins in response to pathogens into our blood to fight with them; these proteins are called antibodies; each antibody molecule has four peptide chains, two small called light chains and two longer called heavy chains; hence, an antibody is represented as H₂L₂; different types of antibodies are produced in our body: IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG are some of them. When a host is exposed to antigens, which may be in the form of living or dead microbes or other proteins, antibodies are produced in the host body; this type of immunity is called active immunity; when ready-made antibodies are directly given to protect the body against foreign agents, it is called passive immunity; the yellowish fluid colostrum secreted by the mother during the initial days of lactation has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant; for snakebites, the injection given to patients contains preformed antibodies against the snake venom.
Why: Memory cells make the second response faster and stronger, while transferred antibodies act immediately but are not replenished.
Why not the others: (A) A vaccine stimulates the person's own response (active). (B) Antivenom gives passive immunity without memory. (D) Antibodies have four chains.
Key point: Active (own response, memory) vs passive (ready-made antibodies); H₂L₂.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the design features of a stirred-tank bioreactor and the steps of downstream processing for a recombinant product
questions.question: Which explanation of bioreactors and downstream processing is correct?
options: A) Small flasks are preferred for industrial production because they give the most product

B) A stirred-tank bioreactor is usually cylindrical or has a curved base to help mix the contents; the stirrer mixes the contents and keeps oxygen evenly available, while sterile air bubbled in (sparged) greatly increases the surface area for oxygen transfer; the bioreactor provides optimal conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen) and has an agitator, oxygen delivery, foam control, temperature and pH control systems and sampling ports, with volumes of 100–1000 litres; after biosynthesis the product goes through downstream processing — separation and purification (recovery), then formulation with suitable preservatives, followed by clinical trials for drugs and strict quality control
C) Downstream processing means adding the gene of interest to the host cell
D) Sparging removes oxygen from the culture so that cells grow faster
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Stirred-tank design (curved base, stirrer, sparger, control systems); downstream processing: separation, purification, formulation, trials, quality control.
Concept: To produce in large quantities, the development of bioreactors, where large volumes (100–1000 litres) of culture can be processed, was required; thus, bioreactors can be thought of as vessels in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products, individual enzymes, etc., using microbial, plant, animal or human cells; a bioreactor provides the optimal conditions for achieving the desired product by providing optimum growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen). The most commonly used bioreactors are of stirring type; a stirred-tank reactor is usually cylindrical or with a curved base to facilitate the mixing of the reactor contents; the stirrer facilitates even mixing and oxygen availability throughout the bioreactor; alternatively, air can be bubbled through the reactor; the bioreactor has an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system and a foam control system, a temperature control system, a pH control system and sampling ports so that small volumes of the culture can be withdrawn periodically; in the sparged stirred-tank bioreactor, sterile air bubbles are sparged, which greatly increases the area for oxygen transfer. After completion of the biosynthetic stage, the product has to be subjected through a series of processes before it is ready for marketing as a finished product; the processes include separation and purification, which are collectively referred to as downstream processing; the product has to be formulated with suitable preservatives; such formulation has to undergo thorough clinical trials as in case of drugs; strict quality control testing for each product is also required; the downstream processing and quality control testing vary from product to product.
Why: Large cultures need even mixing, enough oxygen and stable conditions to keep cells productive, and the product must then be isolated and made safe.
Why not the others: (A) Large volumes need bioreactors. (C) Inserting the gene is part of earlier steps, not downstream processing. (D) Sparging supplies oxygen.
Key point: Stirred-tank: mixing + sparging for O₂, control systems; downstream = separation, purification, formulation, QC.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing C–X bond length, bond enthalpy, dipole moment, boiling point and density across methyl and alkyl halides
questions.question: Which set of comparisons for haloalkanes is correct?
options: A) Dipole moment CH₃I > CH₃Br > CH₃Cl > CH₃F, because the dipole moment depends only on electronegativity

B) C–X bond length increases and bond enthalpy decreases from C–F to C–I; dipole moments are CH₃Cl (1.860 D) > CH₃F (1.847 D) > CH₃Br (1.830 D) > CH₃I (1.636 D), CH₃F being lower than CH₃Cl because its much shorter bond outweighs the larger charge separation; boiling points rise as RI > RBr > RCl > RF, and for isomers fall with branching (1-bromobutane > 2-bromobutane > 2-bromo-2-methylpropane); density rises with the number and mass of halogen atoms
C) Boiling points increase with branching because branched molecules have larger surface area
D) Haloalkanes are highly soluble in water because the C–X bond is polar
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Bond length and enthalpy trends, dipole order CH₃Cl > CH₃F > CH₃Br > CH₃I, boiling and density trends.
Concept: Halogen atoms are more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polarised, carbon bearing a partial positive charge and halogen a partial negative charge. Since the size of the halogen atom increases down the group, fluorine is the smallest and iodine the largest; consequently the carbon–halogen bond length also increases from C–F to C–I, and the bond enthalpy decreases. Dipole moment is the product of charge and distance; although fluorine is the most electronegative, the C–F bond is so short that the dipole moment of CH₃F is slightly less than that of CH₃Cl. Molecules of organic halogen compounds are generally polar; due to greater polarity as well as higher molecular mass compared to the parent hydrocarbon, intermolecular forces (dipole–dipole and van der Waals) are stronger in halogen derivatives, so boiling points of chlorides, bromides and iodides are considerably higher than those of hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass. For the same alkyl group, boiling points decrease in the order RI > RBr > RCl > RF, because van der Waals forces increase with size and mass of the halogen. For isomeric haloalkanes, boiling points decrease with increase in branching, because branching makes the molecule more compact and reduces surface area. Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives of hydrocarbons are heavier than water; density increases with the number of carbon atoms, halogen atoms and atomic mass of the halogen atoms. Haloalkanes are only very slightly soluble in water: less energy is released when new attractions are set up between haloalkane and water molecules than is needed to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
Given: Dipole moments CH₃F 1.847 D, CH₃Cl 1.860 D, CH₃Br 1.830 D, CH₃I 1.636 D.
Formula/Principle: μ = q × d; boiling point rises with van der Waals forces (mass, surface area).
Step 1: Bond length rises from C–F to C–I, so bond enthalpy falls.
Step 2: μ depends on both q and d; CH₃F has larger q but much smaller d, so μ(CH₃Cl) > μ(CH₃F).
Step 3: Branching reduces surface area, lowering boiling point.
Why: Physical properties depend on both polarity and the size and mass of the halogen, so no single property follows electronegativity alone.
Why not the others: (A) CH₃I has the lowest dipole moment; bond length also matters. (C) Branching reduces surface area and boiling point. (D) Haloalkanes cannot break water's hydrogen bonds strongly enough to dissolve much.
Key point: μ: CH₃Cl > CH₃F > CH₃Br > CH₃I; b.p.: RI > RBr > RCl > RF; branching lowers b.p.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Choosing the carbonyl compound and Grignard reagent that give a particular alcohol, and identifying the products of acid-catalysed hydration and of ester reduction
questions.question:
The following preparations are proposed:

Route | Reactants | Claimed product
I | HCHO + CH₃CH₂MgBr, then H₃O⁺ | Propan-1-ol
II | CH₃COCH₃ + CH₃CH₂MgBr, then H₃O⁺ | 2-Methylbutan-2-ol
III | CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O (dil. H₂SO₄) | Propan-1-ol
IV | CH₃CHO + CH₃MgBr, then H₃O⁺ | Propan-2-ol
V | CH₃COOC₂H₅ + LiAlH₄, then H₂O | Ethanol as the only organic product

How many claims are correct, and what is the correct reasoning?
options: A) All five, since every reagent here adds hydrogen across a double bond
B) Two (I and IV); II gives a secondary alcohol and V gives methanol
