questions.question: The triangle with vertices \((k,0),(4,0),(0,2)\) has area 4 square units. Find \(k\), find \(x\) so that \((1,2),(3,8),(x,14)\) are collinear, and the equation of the line through \((1,2)\) and \((3,6)\) using determinants.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(k=0\text{ or }8;\ x=5;\ y=2x\)
Concept: \(\Delta=\dfrac12\begin{vmatrix}x_1&y_1&1\\x_2&y_2&1\\x_3&y_3&1\end{vmatrix},\ \text{area is }|\Delta|;\ \text{three points are collinear iff this determinant is }0;\ \text{the line through two points is obtained by taking the third point as }(x,y)\)
Given: \((k,0),(4,0),(0,2),\ \text{area}=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\pm4=\dfrac12\begin{vmatrix}k&0&1\\4&0&1\\0&2&1\end{vmatrix}\)
Step 1: \(\text{expand: }k(0-2)-0+1(8-0)=8-2k\Rightarrow \tfrac12(8-2k)=\pm4\Rightarrow k=0\text{ or }8\)
Step 2: \(1(8-14)-2(3-x)+1(42-8x)=-6-6+2x+42-8x=30-6x=0\Rightarrow x=5\)
Step 3: \(\begin{vmatrix}x&y&1\\1&2&1\\3&6&1\end{vmatrix}=x(2-6)-y(1-3)+(6-6)=-4x+2y=0\Rightarrow y=2x\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac12\left|\begin{matrix}8&0&1\\4&0&1\\0&2&1\end{matrix}\right|=\frac12\,|8(-2)+1(8)|=\frac12\cdot8=4\]
Check: \[k=0:\ \text{base from }(0,0)\text{ to }(4,0)=4,\ \text{height }2,\ \text{area}=4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the area condition carries a modulus, so both signs of the determinant must be taken}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses }k=0\text{ and the line is wrong}\); (C) \(k=-4\text{ gives area }8;\ (1,2)\text{ is not on }y=2x+1\); (D) \(k=-8\text{ gives area }12\).
Key point: \(\text{area}=|\Delta|\Rightarrow\text{two values};\ \Delta=0\Rightarrow\text{collinear}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding first and second derivatives of curves given parametrically and slopes of tangents at given parameter values
questions.question: Find the slope of the tangent to the astroid \(x=a\cos^3\theta,\ y=a\sin^3\theta\) at \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\), the slope of the tangent to the cycloid \(x=a(\theta-\sin\theta),\ y=a(1-\cos\theta)\) at \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\), and \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) for \(x=at^2,\ y=2at\).
options: C) \(\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4};\ \sqrt3;\ -\dfrac{1}{at}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(-1;\ 1;\ -\dfrac{1}{2at^3}\)
Concept: \(\text{If }x=f(t),\ y=g(t),\ \text{then }\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\ (dx/dt\ne0),\ \text{and }\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\!\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)\Big/\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)
Given: \(\text{astroid, cycloid, parabola in parametric form}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\dot y}{\dot x}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3a\sin^2\theta\cos\theta}{-3a\cos^2\theta\sin\theta}=-\tan\theta=-1\text{ at }\tfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{a\sin\theta}{a(1-\cos\theta)}=\cot\tfrac{\theta}{2}=1\text{ at }\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2a}{2at}=\dfrac1t;\ \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{-1/t^2}{2at}=-\dfrac{1}{2at^3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta}=\frac{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}}{2\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}}=\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\]
Check: \[y^2=4ax\Rightarrow 2yy'=4a\Rightarrow y'=\frac{2a}{y}=\frac1t;\ y''=-\frac{2a}{y^2}y'=-\frac{2a}{4a^2t^2}\cdot\frac1t=-\frac{1}{2at^3}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the second derivative must be divided again by }dx/dt,\ \text{because }d/dx\text{ is not }d/dt\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{signs wrong}\); (B) \(\text{cycloid slope is 1; forgot to divide by }dx/dt\); (C) \(\text{astroid slope is negative; cycloid slope wrong}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{d}{dt}(y')\div\dfrac{dx}{dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Relating rates of change of volume, depth and surface area of water poured into an inverted conical tank using similar triangles
questions.question: Water is poured at \(5\text{ cm}^3\text{ s}^{-1}\) into an inverted cone of height 10 cm and base radius 5 cm. When the depth is 4 cm, how fast is the depth rising and how fast is the area of the water surface increasing?
options: A) \(\dfrac{5}{16\pi}\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ \dfrac58\text{ cm}^2\text{ s}^{-1}\)
B) \(\dfrac{5}{4\pi}\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ \dfrac52\text{ cm}^2\text{ s}^{-1}\)
C) \(\dfrac{5}{\pi}\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ 10\text{ cm}^2\text{ s}^{-1}\)
D) \(\dfrac{15}{16\pi}\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ \dfrac{15}{4}\text{ cm}^2\text{ s}^{-1}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{5}{4\pi}\text{ cm s}^{-1},\ \dfrac{dA}{dt}=\dfrac52\text{ cm}^2\text{ s}^{-1}\)
Concept: \(\text{When related quantities change with time, differentiate the relation between them with respect to }t\ (\text{chain rule}),\ \text{expressing all variables through one by geometry first}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=5,\ H=10,\ R=5,\ h=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{similar triangles }\dfrac rh=\dfrac RH=\dfrac12;\ V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h\)
Step 1: \(r=\tfrac h2\Rightarrow V=\tfrac13\pi\cdot\tfrac{h^2}{4}\cdot h=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{4}\dfrac{dh}{dt}\Rightarrow 5=\dfrac{16\pi}{4}\dfrac{dh}{dt}\Rightarrow\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{5}{4\pi}\)
Step 3: \(A=\pi r^2=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{4}\Rightarrow\dfrac{dA}{dt}=\dfrac{\pi h}{2}\dfrac{dh}{dt}=2\pi\cdot\dfrac{5}{4\pi}=\dfrac52\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\pi h^3}{12}\right)=\frac{3\pi h^2}{12}\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{\pi h^2}{4}\frac{dh}{dt}=A\,\frac{dh}{dt}\]
Check: \[A(4)=\pi\cdot2^2=4\pi;\ A\,\frac{dh}{dt}=4\pi\cdot\frac{5}{4\pi}=5=\frac{dV}{dt}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the inflow spreads over the current surface area, so the depth rises at }\tfrac{dV/dt}{A}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{used }r=h\text{ wrongly scaled}\); (C) \(\text{ignores the cone shape}\); (D) \(\text{used }3\pi h^2/12\text{ incorrectly with }r=h\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=A\,\dfrac{dh}{dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the fundamental theorem of calculus to find an unknown limit of integration and to differentiate an integral with a variable upper limit
questions.question: Find all real \(k\) with \(\displaystyle\int_0^k(2x+1)\,dx=6\), the value of \(a>1\) with \(\displaystyle\int_1^a\frac{dx}{x}=2\), and \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_0^{x^2}\cos t\,dt\).
options: B) \(k=2\text{ only};\ a=\sqrt e;\ 2x\sin x^2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(k=2\text{ or }-3;\ a=e^2;\ 2x\cos x^2\)
Concept: \(\text{FTC: if }F'=f\text{ then }\int_a^bf=F(b)-F(a);\ \text{and }\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_a^{g(x)}f(t)\,dt=f(g(x))\,g'(x)\)
Given: \(\text{the three conditions}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)\)
Step 1: \([x^2+x]_0^k=k^2+k=6\Rightarrow(k+3)(k-2)=0\Rightarrow k=2,-3\)
Step 2: \([\ln x]_1^a=\ln a=2\Rightarrow a=e^2\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[\sin t\big]_0^{x^2}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x^2=2x\cos x^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^{-3}(2x+1)\,dx=\big[x^2+x\big]_0^{-3}=9-3=6\]
Check: \[\int_0^2(2x+1)\,dx=4+2=6;\ \ln e^2=2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the integral is a function of its limit, so the condition becomes an ordinary equation in }k\)
Why not the others: (A) \(9+3\ne6;\ \text{chain-rule factor missing}\); (B) \(-3\text{ also works; derivative of }\sin\text{ is }\cos\); (D) \(\text{roots have wrong signs; factor }2x\text{ missing}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\int_a^{g(x)}f=f(g)\,g'\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating definite integrals using the property ∫₀^a f(x) dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x) dx in three different settings
questions.question: Evaluate \(I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{\sin x+\cos x}\,dx\), \(I_2=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx\) and \(I_3=\displaystyle\int_0^{1}x(1-x)^5\,dx\).
options: B) \(\tfrac{\pi}{2};\ \tfrac{\pi^2}{2};\ \tfrac16\)
D) \(\tfrac{\pi}{4};\ \tfrac{\pi}{2};\ \tfrac1{7}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(I_1=\tfrac{\pi}{4},\ I_2=\tfrac{\pi^2}{4},\ I_3=\tfrac1{42}\)
Concept: \(\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^af(a-x)\,dx;\ \text{replacing }x\text{ by }a-x\text{ either produces a companion integral that adds to something simple, or removes an awkward factor}\)
Given: \(\text{the three integrals}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin(\tfrac{\pi}{2}-x)=\cos x;\ \sin(\pi-x)=\sin x,\ \cos(\pi-x)=-\cos x\)
Step 1: \(I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x}{\cos x+\sin x}dx\Rightarrow2I_1=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow I_1=\tfrac{\pi}{4}\)
Step 2: \(I_2=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{(\pi-x)\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx\Rightarrow2I_2=\pi\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx=\pi\big[-\tan^{-1}(\cos x)\big]_0^{\pi}=\pi\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow I_2=\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}\)
Step 3: \(I_3=\displaystyle\int_0^1(1-x)x^5\,dx=\tfrac16-\tfrac17=\tfrac1{42}\)
Worked derivation: \[\big[-\tan^{-1}(\cos x)\big]_0^{\pi}=-\tan^{-1}(-1)+\tan^{-1}(1)=\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}\]
Check: \[I_3\text{ by expansion would need six terms; the swap gives }\int_0^1(x^5-x^6)\,dx=\frac{7-6}{42}=\frac1{42}>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the property moves the troublesome factor (the }x\text{ or the power) onto the simpler part of the integrand}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{forgot to halve after adding}\); (C) \(I_1\ne1;\ I_2\text{ needs the }\pi\text{ factor}\); (D) \(I_2,I_3\text{ miscomputed}\).
Key point: \(\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^af(a-x)\,dx\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using the phase of simple harmonic motion to find the initial phase, the time between two displacements and the speed at a given displacement, and how these scale with amplitude
questions.question: A particle executes SHM \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)\) with \(A=4\text{ cm}\) and \(T=2\text{ s}\). At \(t=0\) it is at \(x=2\text{ cm}\) moving away from the mean position. What are \(\phi\), the time to reach \(x=4\text{ cm}\) for the first time, and its speed at \(x=2\text{ cm}\)? If \(A\) is doubled, what happens to \(T\) and to the maximum speed?
options: A) \(\tfrac{\pi}{3};\ \tfrac12\text{ s};\ 2\pi\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ T\text{ doubles}\)
B) \(\tfrac{\pi}{6};\ \tfrac13\text{ s};\ 2\sqrt3\,\pi\approx10.9\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ T\text{ unchanged, }v_{\max}\text{ doubles}\)
C) \(\tfrac{\pi}{6};\ \tfrac16\text{ s};\ 4\pi\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ T\text{ unchanged, }v_{\max}\text{ unchanged}\)
D) \(\tfrac{5\pi}{6};\ \tfrac23\text{ s};\ 2\sqrt3\,\pi\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ T\text{ halves}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\phi=\tfrac{\pi}{6},\ t=\tfrac13\text{ s},\ v=2\sqrt3\,\pi\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ T\text{ unchanged},\ v_{\max}\text{ doubles}\)
Given: \(A=4\text{ cm},\ T=2\text{ s}\Rightarrow\omega=\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ x(0)=2\text{ cm},\ v(0)>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi),\ v=\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2},\ T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\ (\text{independent of }A)\)
Step 1: \(\sin\phi=\tfrac12,\ v(0)=A\omega\cos\phi>0\Rightarrow\phi=\tfrac{\pi}{6}\)
Step 2: \(\text{reach }x=A\text{ when phase}=\tfrac{\pi}{2}:\ \omega t=\tfrac{\pi}{2}-\tfrac{\pi}{6}=\tfrac{\pi}{3}\Rightarrow t=\tfrac13\text{ s}\)
Step 3: \(v=\pi\sqrt{16-4}=2\sqrt3\,\pi\approx10.9\text{ cm s}^{-1};\ v_{\max}=A\omega\propto A\)
Worked derivation: \[t=\frac{\Delta\phi}{\omega}=\frac{\pi/3}{\pi}=\frac13\ \text{s}=\frac{T}{6}\]
Check: \[x\!\left(\tfrac13\right)=4\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}+\tfrac{\pi}{6}\right)=4\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}=4\ \text{cm}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{phase grows uniformly at rate }\omega,\ \text{so the time between two states is their phase difference divided by }\omega\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}\ne\tfrac12;\ T\text{ does not depend on }A\); (C) \(\text{time and speed wrong; }v_{\max}=A\omega\text{ doubles}\); (D) \(\phi=\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\text{ means moving towards the mean}\).
Key point: \(\Delta t=\Delta\phi/\omega;\ T\text{ independent of amplitude}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Phase change on reflection from fixed and free ends, formation of stationary waves by superposition, and how harmonic frequencies of a stretched string scale with tension
questions.question: A string 1.0 m long, fixed at both ends, carries transverse waves at \(200\text{ m s}^{-1}\). What are its fundamental frequency and third harmonic, what happens to them if the tension is made four times, and what is the result of superposing \(y_1=a\sin(kx-\omega t)\) and \(y_2=a\sin(kx+\omega t)\)?
options: A) \(200\text{ Hz};\ 600\text{ Hz};\ \text{unchanged};\ \text{a travelling wave of amplitude }2a\)
B) \(100\text{ Hz};\ 200\text{ Hz};\ \text{four times};\ 2a\cos kx\sin\omega t\)
C) \(50\text{ Hz};\ 150\text{ Hz};\ \text{halved};\ \text{zero everywhere}\)

D) \(100\text{ Hz};\ 300\text{ Hz};\ \text{doubled (200 Hz, 600 Hz)};\ y=2a\sin kx\cos\omega t,\ \text{a stationary wave with nodes }\lambda/2\text{ apart; reflection at a fixed end reverses the phase by }\pi,\ \text{at a free end there is no phase change}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(100\text{ Hz},\ 300\text{ Hz};\ \text{both double};\ y=2a\sin kx\cos\omega t\)
Given: \(L=1.0\text{ m},\ v=200\text{ m s}^{-1};\ T\to4T\)
Formula/Principle: \(f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L};\ v=\sqrt{T/\mu};\ \sin(A)+\sin(B)=2\sin\tfrac{A+B}{2}\cos\tfrac{A-B}{2}\)
Step 1: \(f_1=\dfrac{200}{2}=100\text{ Hz},\ f_3=300\text{ Hz}\)
Step 2: \(T\times4\Rightarrow v\times2\Rightarrow f_n\times2\)
Step 3: \(y_1+y_2=2a\sin kx\cos\omega t;\ \text{nodes where }\sin kx=0\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{n\lambda}{2}\)
Worked derivation: \[y=a[\sin(kx-\omega t)+\sin(kx+\omega t)]=2a\sin\frac{2kx}{2}\cos\frac{-2\omega t}{2}=2a\sin kx\cos\omega t\]
Check: \[\lambda_1=2L=2\text{ m},\ f_1=\frac{v}{\lambda_1}=100\text{ Hz};\ \text{at }x=0:\ y=0\ (\text{node at the fixed end})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a wave and its reflection travelling oppositely superpose into a pattern whose shape does not move, with nodes forced at fixed ends}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f_1=v/2L;\ \text{superposition gives a stationary wave}\); (B) \(f_3=3f_1;\ f\propto\sqrt T\); (C) \(\text{frequency formula wrong; waves do not cancel everywhere}\).
Key point: \(f_n=nv/2L,\ v\propto\sqrt T;\ \text{opposite waves}\to\text{stationary wave}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Measuring the change in Coulomb force when two identical charged conducting spheres are touched and separated, and the net force on a charge at a vertex of an equilateral triangle by superposition
questions.question: Two identical small conducting spheres carry \(+6\ \mu\text{C}\) and \(-2\ \mu\text{C}\) and are held \(0.30\text{ m}\) apart. They are touched together and returned to the same separation. Separately, three equal charges \(q\) sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side \(a\); let \(F_0=\dfrac{kq^2}{a^2}\). What are the forces before and after touching, and the net force on one charge of the triangle? (\(k=9\times10^9\text{ N m}^2\text{ C}^{-2}\))
options: A) \(1.2\text{ N attractive};\ 0.4\text{ N repulsive (each sphere }+2\ \mu\text{C)};\ \sqrt3F_0\text{ along the bisector, away from the triangle}\)
B) \(1.2\text{ N repulsive};\ 1.2\text{ N attractive};\ 2F_0\)
C) \(0.4\text{ N attractive};\ 1.2\text{ N repulsive};\ F_0\)
D) \(1.2\text{ N attractive};\ 0;\ 0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1.2\text{ N attractive};\ 0.4\text{ N repulsive};\ \sqrt3F_0\)
Given: \(q_1=+6\ \mu\text{C},\ q_2=-2\ \mu\text{C},\ r=0.30\text{ m};\ \text{triangle side }a\)
Formula/Principle: \(F=\dfrac{k|q_1q_2|}{r^2};\ \text{charge conservation};\ \text{vector superposition}\)
Step 1: \(F_1=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times12\times10^{-12}}{0.09}=1.2\text{ N (attractive)}\)
Step 2: \(\text{total }+4\ \mu\text{C shared equally}\Rightarrow+2\ \mu\text{C each};\ F_2=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times4\times10^{-12}}{0.09}=0.4\text{ N (repulsive)}\)
Step 3: \(\text{two forces }F_0\text{ at }60^\circ:\ F=2F_0\cos30^\circ=\sqrt3F_0\)
Worked derivation: \[F_{\text{net}}=\sqrt{F_0^2+F_0^2+2F_0^2\cos60^\circ}=\sqrt{3}\,F_0\]
Check: \[\frac{F_2}{F_1}=\frac{2\times2}{6\times2}=\frac13,\ \ \frac{1.2}{3}=0.4\ \text{N}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{identical conductors in contact share the total charge equally, and forces from several charges add as vectors}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{unlike charges attract first; like charges repel after}\); (C) \(\text{magnitudes swapped}\); (D) \(\text{net charge }+4\ \mu\text{C remains, so force is not zero}\).
Key point: \(\text{conservation of charge on contact};\ F\text{ adds vectorially}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the potential of an electric dipole at axial, equatorial and oblique points, and the work done in moving a charge along the equatorial line
questions.question: A dipole consists of \(\pm5\text{ nC}\) separated by \(4\text{ mm}\). At \(r=0.20\text{ m}\) from its centre (\(r\gg\) separation), what is the potential on the axis, on the equatorial line, and at \(60^\circ\) from the axis? How much work is needed to move \(1\ \mu\text{C}\) between two points on the equatorial line?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(V_{\text{axis}}=4.5\text{ V},\ V_{\text{eq}}=0,\ V_{60^\circ}=2.25\text{ V};\ W=0\)
Given: \(q=5\times10^{-9}\text{ C},\ 2a=4\times10^{-3}\text{ m},\ r=0.20\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(p=q(2a);\ V=\dfrac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}\ (r\gg a);\ W=q\Delta V\)
Step 1: \(p=5\times10^{-9}\times4\times10^{-3}=2\times10^{-11}\text{ C m}\)
Step 2: \(V_{\text{axis}}=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-11}}{0.04}=4.5\text{ V};\ \theta=90^\circ\Rightarrow V=0\)
Step 3: \(V_{60^\circ}=4.5\cos60^\circ=2.25\text{ V};\ \text{equatorial line is equipotential}\Rightarrow W=0\)
Worked derivation: \[V=kq\left(\frac{1}{r-a\cos\theta}-\frac{1}{r+a\cos\theta}\right)\approx\frac{kq\,2a\cos\theta}{r^2}=\frac{kp\cos\theta}{r^2}\]
Check: \[\text{on the equatorial line each point is equidistant from }+q\text{ and }-q\Rightarrow V=kq/r_1-kq/r_1=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{dipole potential depends on }\cos\theta,\ \text{largest on the axis and zero where the two charges are equally far}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(V_{\text{eq}}=0;\ \text{no work on an equipotential}\); (B) \(V\text{ depends on }\theta\); (D) \(\text{axis and equator swapped}\).
Key point: \(V=kp\cos\theta/r^2;\ \text{equatorial plane is equipotential at }V=0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using the linear temperature dependence of resistivity to find resistance at a higher temperature and the temperature for a given resistance, the effect of stretching a wire at constant volume, and the behaviour of semiconductors
questions.question: A copper wire has resistance \(10.0\ \Omega\) at \(20^\circ\text{C}\) with \(\alpha=4.0\times10^{-3}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\). Find its resistance at \(120^\circ\text{C}\) and the temperature at which it is \(12.0\ \Omega\). If the wire is stretched to twice its length (volume constant), what is its resistance at \(20^\circ\text{C}\)? How does a semiconductor's resistivity change on heating?
options: A) \(10.4\ \Omega;\ 50^\circ\text{C};\ 20\ \Omega;\ \text{increases}\)
B) \(14.8\ \Omega;\ 100^\circ\text{C};\ 5\ \Omega;\ \text{unchanged}\)
C) \(4.0\ \Omega;\ 70^\circ\text{C};\ 40\ \Omega;\ \text{increases}\)
D) \(14.0\ \Omega;\ 70^\circ\text{C};\ 40\ \Omega;\ \text{decreases (more charge carriers; negative temperature coefficient)}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(14.0\ \Omega;\ 70^\circ\text{C};\ 40\ \Omega;\ \text{decreases}\)
Given: \(R_0=10.0\ \Omega\text{ at }T_0=20^\circ\text{C},\ \alpha=4.0\times10^{-3}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(R_T=R_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)];\ R=\rho\dfrac{l}{A},\ Al=\text{constant}\Rightarrow R\propto l^2\)
Step 1: \(R_{120}=10[1+4\times10^{-3}\times100]=14.0\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(12=10[1+4\times10^{-3}(T-20)]\Rightarrow T-20=50\Rightarrow T=70^\circ\text{C}\)
Step 3: \(l\to2l,\ A\to A/2\Rightarrow R\to4R=40\ \Omega\)
Worked derivation: \[R'=\rho\frac{2l}{A/2}=4\rho\frac{l}{A}=4R\]
Check: \[R_{70}=10(1+0.004\times50)=10\times1.2=12.0\ \Omega\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in metals more frequent collisions at higher temperature raise resistivity, while in semiconductors the number density of carriers rises sharply}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\alpha\Delta T=0.4,\ \text{not }0.04;\ R\propto l^2\); (B) \(\text{arithmetic wrong; semiconductor resistivity falls}\); (C) \(\text{resistance cannot fall on heating copper}\).
Key point: \(R_T=R_0(1+\alpha\Delta T);\ \text{stretch }n\text{ times}\Rightarrow n^2R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the motion of charged particles in crossed electric and magnetic fields (velocity selector), why the magnetic force does no work, and the paths in a uniform magnetic field
questions.question: Which statement about charged particles in electric and magnetic fields is correct?
options: A) In crossed fields with \(\vec E\perp\vec B\perp\vec v\), a particle passes undeflected when \(qE=qvB\), i.e. \(v=E/B\), independent of its charge and mass, so the arrangement selects speeds; faster particles are deflected towards the side of the magnetic force; the magnetic force \(q\vec v\times\vec B\) is always perpendicular to \(\vec v\), so it does no work and cannot change the speed; in a uniform \(\vec B\), a particle moving perpendicular to it describes a circle of radius \(mv/qB\), one moving parallel goes straight, and one moving at an angle follows a helix
B) The magnetic force increases the kinetic energy of a charged particle moving in a circle
C) A velocity selector passes only particles of a particular mass
D) A charge moving parallel to \(\vec B\) describes a circle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(v=E/B\) selected; magnetic force does no work; circle, straight line or helix.
Given: \(\text{crossed uniform }\vec E\text{ and }\vec B;\ \text{charge }q,\ \text{velocity }\vec v\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec F=q(\vec E+\vec v\times\vec B)\ (\text{Lorentz force});\ r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}\)
Step 1: \(\text{electric force }qE\text{ and magnetic force }qvB\text{ opposite}\Rightarrow\text{balance at }v=E/B\)
Step 2: \(v>E/B\Rightarrow qvB>qE\Rightarrow\text{deflected along the magnetic force}\)
Step 3: \(\vec F_B\perp\vec v\Rightarrow P=\vec F_B\cdot\vec v=0\Rightarrow\text{speed constant}\)
Worked derivation: \[qvB=\frac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow r=\frac{mv}{qB},\quad T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}\]
Check: \[\vec v\parallel\vec B\Rightarrow\vec v\times\vec B=0\Rightarrow\text{no force, straight line}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the electric force does not depend on speed while the magnetic force does, so only one speed balances them}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{magnetic force does no work}\); (C) \(\text{selection is by speed, not mass}\); (D) \(\text{parallel motion feels no magnetic force}\).
Key point: \(v=E/B;\ \text{magnetic force changes direction, not speed}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting probe readings of a magnetic field between the plates of a charging capacitor, and calculating the rate of change of electric field needed for a given displacement current
questions.question: A parallel-plate capacitor with plate area \(0.010\text{ m}^2\) is charged by a steady current of \(1.0\text{ A}\). A small magnetic-field probe placed in the gap, off the axis, records a field circling the axis, just as near the connecting wire; after the capacitor is fully charged and the current stops, the reading falls to zero. Which interpretation is correct? (\(\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{ N}^{-1}\text{ m}^{-2}\))
options: A) No charge crosses the gap, so the probe reading must be an error
B) The field in the gap is produced by charges leaking across the gap

C) A changing electric flux in the gap gives a displacement current \(i_d=\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}\), equal to the conduction current in the wires, so Ampere–Maxwell's law \(\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0(i_c+i_d)\) predicts a magnetic field in the gap; here \(\dfrac{dE}{dt}=\dfrac{i}{\varepsilon_0A}\approx1.1\times10^{13}\text{ V m}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}\); when charging stops, \(E\) is constant, \(i_d=0\), and the field vanishes
D) The displacement current remains after charging stops because the electric field is still present
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\text{Displacement current }i_d=i_c\text{ during charging};\ dE/dt\approx1.1\times10^{13}\text{ V m}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1};\ \text{zero when }E\text{ is steady}\)
Given: \(A=0.010\text{ m}^2,\ i=1.0\text{ A}\)
Formula/Principle: \(i_d=\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}=\varepsilon_0A\dfrac{dE}{dt};\ \oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0(i_c+i_d)\)
Step 1: \(E=\dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{dE}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0A}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=\dfrac{i}{\varepsilon_0A}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dE}{dt}=\dfrac{1.0}{8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.010}=1.13\times10^{13}\text{ V m}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(\text{fully charged}\Rightarrow dE/dt=0\Rightarrow i_d=0\Rightarrow B=0\text{ in the gap}\)
Worked derivation: \[i_d=\varepsilon_0A\frac{dE}{dt}=\varepsilon_0A\cdot\frac{i}{\varepsilon_0A}=i\]
Check: \[8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.010\times1.13\times10^{13}=1.0\ \text{A}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{Ampere's law must give the same field for any surface bounded by the loop, which requires a current-like term where the electric flux changes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the reading is real and predicted by Maxwell}\); (B) \(\text{no conduction current crosses an ideal gap}\); (D) \(i_d\text{ depends on the rate of change, not the value, of }E\).
Key point: \(i_d=\varepsilon_0\,d\Phi_E/dt;\ \text{steady }E\Rightarrow i_d=0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing image position, nature and magnification for an object placed inside the focal length of a concave mirror and in front of a convex mirror of the same focal length
questions.question: An object is placed \(10\text{ cm}\) in front of (i) a concave mirror and (ii) a convex mirror, each of focal length \(15\text{ cm}\). Using the Cartesian sign convention, which comparison is correct?
options: A) \(\text{(i) }v=-30\text{ cm, real, }m=-3;\ \text{(ii) }v=-6\text{ cm, real, }m=-0.6\)
B) \(\text{(i) }v=+30\text{ cm, virtual, erect, }m=+3\ (\text{magnified});\ \text{(ii) }v=+6\text{ cm, virtual, erect, }m=+0.6\ (\text{diminished});\ \text{both images lie behind the mirror}\)
C) \(\text{(i) }v=+6\text{ cm, }m=+0.6;\ \text{(ii) }v=+30\text{ cm, }m=+3\)
D) \(\text{(i) no image is formed};\ \text{(ii) }v=+6\text{ cm}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\text{concave: }v=+30\text{ cm},\ m=+3;\ \text{convex: }v=+6\text{ cm},\ m=+0.6\)
Given: \(u=-10\text{ cm};\ f_{\text{concave}}=-15\text{ cm},\ f_{\text{convex}}=+15\text{ cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v+\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f;\ m=-\dfrac vu\)
Step 1: \(\text{concave: }\dfrac1v=-\dfrac1{15}+\dfrac1{10}=\dfrac1{30}\Rightarrow v=+30\text{ cm}\)
Step 2: \(m=-\dfrac{30}{-10}=+3\Rightarrow\text{virtual, erect, magnified}\)
Step 3: \(\text{convex: }\dfrac1v=\dfrac1{15}+\dfrac1{10}=\dfrac16\Rightarrow v=+6\text{ cm},\ m=+0.6\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac1v=\frac1f-\frac1u=\frac{1}{-15}-\frac{1}{-10}=\frac{-2+3}{30}=\frac{1}{30}\]
Check: \[\text{convex: }\frac16+\frac1{-10}=\frac{5-3}{30}=\frac1{15}=\frac1f\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{inside }F\text{ the concave mirror cannot converge the reflected rays, so they appear to diverge from a point behind it, like a convex mirror but magnified}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{signs wrong; both images are virtual}\); (C) \(\text{results swapped}\); (D) \(\text{a concave mirror forms a virtual image for an object inside }F\).
Key point: \(\text{object inside }F\text{ of concave}\Rightarrow\text{virtual, magnified; convex always virtual, diminished}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Scaling the Bohr radius, orbital speed and energy with principal quantum number n and atomic number Z for hydrogen-like ions
questions.question: For hydrogen in its ground state \(r_1=0.53\text{ Å}\), \(v_1=2.18\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1}\), \(E_1=-13.6\text{ eV}\). For \(\text{He}^+\) (\(Z=2\)) in \(n=2\), what are the radius, speed and energy, and how does the orbital period scale?
options: A) \(1.06\text{ Å};\ 2.18\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1};\ -13.6\text{ eV};\ T\propto\dfrac{n^3}{Z^2}\)
B) \(0.53\text{ Å};\ 4.36\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1};\ -27.2\text{ eV};\ T\propto n^2Z\)
C) \(2.12\text{ Å};\ 1.09\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1};\ -3.4\text{ eV};\ T\propto\dfrac{n}{Z}\)
D) \(0.265\text{ Å};\ 2.18\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1};\ -54.4\text{ eV};\ T\propto\dfrac{Z^2}{n^3}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(r=1.06\text{ Å},\ v=2.18\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1},\ E=-13.6\text{ eV};\ T\propto n^3/Z^2\)
Given: \(Z=2,\ n=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(r_n=r_1\dfrac{n^2}{Z},\ v_n=v_1\dfrac{Z}{n},\ E_n=E_1\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\)
Step 1: \(r=0.53\times\dfrac{4}{2}=1.06\text{ Å}\)
Step 2: \(v=2.18\times10^6\times\dfrac22=2.18\times10^6\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(E=-13.6\times\dfrac44=-13.6\text{ eV};\ T=\dfrac{2\pi r}{v}\propto\dfrac{n^2/Z}{Z/n}=\dfrac{n^3}{Z^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{kZe^2}{r^2},\ mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi}\Rightarrow v=\frac{2\pi kZe^2}{nh},\ r=\frac{n^2h^2}{4\pi^2mkZe^2}\]
Check: \[E=-\tfrac12mv^2\Rightarrow\text{same }v\Rightarrow\text{same }E=-13.6\text{ eV}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a larger nuclear charge pulls the electron closer and faster, while a higher orbit pushes it out and slows it}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{radius scales as }n^2/Z\); (C) \(\text{ignores }Z\); (D) \(\text{scalings inverted}\).
Key point: \(r\propto n^2/Z,\ v\propto Z/n,\ E\propto Z^2/n^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the mass defect and binding energy per nucleon of helium-4 from measured atomic masses, and relating the binding-energy curve to fission and fusion
questions.question: Mass-spectrometer measurements give \(m(^1\text{H})=1.007825\text{ u}\), \(m_n=1.008665\text{ u}\), \(m(^4\text{He})=4.002603\text{ u}\) (\(1\text{ u}=931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2\)). What are the mass defect, total binding energy and binding energy per nucleon of \(^4\text{He}\), and which statement about the binding-energy curve is correct?
options: A) \(0.0304\text{ u};\ 7.07\text{ MeV};\ 1.77\text{ MeV};\ \text{curve rises steadily with }A\)
B) \(0.0152\text{ u};\ 14.2\text{ MeV};\ 3.5\text{ MeV};\ \text{fission of light nuclei releases energy}\)
C) \(4.0326\text{ u};\ 3756\text{ MeV};\ 939\text{ MeV};\ \text{curve is flat}\)

D) \(0.0304\text{ u};\ 28.3\text{ MeV};\ 7.07\text{ MeV};\ \text{the curve peaks near }A\approx56\ (\approx8.75\text{ MeV}),\ \text{so fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both release energy}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\Delta m=0.0304\text{ u},\ E_b=28.3\text{ MeV},\ E_b/A=7.07\text{ MeV}\)
Given: \(Z=2,\ N=2,\ \text{masses above}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta m=Zm_H+Nm_n-M;\ E_b=\Delta m\,c^2\)
Step 1: \(2(1.007825)+2(1.008665)=4.032980\text{ u}\)
Step 2: \(\Delta m=4.032980-4.002603=0.030377\text{ u}\)
Step 3: \(E_b=0.030377\times931.5=28.30\text{ MeV};\ E_b/A=7.07\text{ MeV}\)
Worked derivation: \[E_b=(2m_H+2m_n-M_{\text{He}})\times931.5\ \text{MeV/u}=0.030377\times931.5\approx28.3\ \text{MeV}\]
Check: \[\frac{28.3}{4}=7.07\ \text{MeV, close to the known value for }^4\text{He}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{energy is released whenever nucleons move to nuclei of higher binding energy per nucleon, towards the peak near iron}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{per-nucleon value taken as total}\); (B) \(\Delta m\text{ halved; fission of light nuclei absorbs energy}\); (C) \(\text{used total mass, not the defect}\).
Key point: \(E_b=\Delta m\times931.5\text{ MeV};\ \text{peak at }A\approx56\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying significant-figure rules to multiplication and addition results and counting significant figures in measured values with zeros
questions.question: A rectangle measures \(4.234\text{ m}\times1.005\text{ m}\). Three masses \(436.32\text{ g}\), \(227.2\text{ g}\) and \(0.301\text{ g}\) are added. How many significant figures are in \(0.0070\) and in \(6.320\)? Which set is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(4.255\text{ m}^2;\ 663.8\text{ g};\ 2;\ 4\)
Given: \(4.234\ (4\text{ s.f.}),\ 1.005\ (4\text{ s.f.});\ 436.32,\ 227.2,\ 0.301\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{product: as many s.f. as the least precise factor; sum: as many decimal places as the least precise term; leading zeros are not significant, trailing zeros after a decimal point are}\)
Step 1: \(4.234\times1.005=4.25517\Rightarrow4.255\text{ m}^2\ (4\text{ s.f.})\)
Step 2: \(436.32+227.2+0.301=663.821\Rightarrow663.8\text{ g}\ (1\text{ decimal place})\)
Step 3: \(0.0070:\ \text{digits }7,0\Rightarrow2;\ 6.320\Rightarrow4\)
Worked derivation: \[4.234\times1.005=4.234+0.02117=4.25517\approx4.255\]
Check: \[227.2\text{ is known only to }0.1\text{ g, so the sum cannot be quoted beyond }0.1\text{ g}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a result cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement that went into it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{results not rounded; }0.0070\text{ has 2 s.f.}\); (C) \(\text{over-rounded}\); (D) \(\text{product to 3 s.f. and sum to 2 decimals are wrong}\).
Key point: \(\times,\div\to\text{least s.f.};\ +,-\to\text{least decimal places}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the scalar and vector products of two vectors, the angle between them, the projection of one on the other and the area of the parallelogram they span
questions.question: For \(\vec A=\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k\) and \(\vec B=2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k\), find \(\vec A\cdot\vec B\), \(\cos\theta\), \(\vec A\times\vec B\), the area of the parallelogram on \(\vec A\) and \(\vec B\), and the projection of \(\vec A\) on \(\vec B\).
options: A) \(8;\ \tfrac89;\ 6\hat i-2\hat j+5\hat k;\ 9;\ \tfrac83\)
C) \(4;\ \tfrac49;\ 6\hat i+2\hat j-5\hat k;\ \sqrt{65};\ \tfrac43\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(4;\ \tfrac49;\ 6\hat i+2\hat j-5\hat k;\ \sqrt{65};\ \tfrac43\)
Given: \(\vec A=(1,2,2),\ \vec B=(2,-1,2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\vec A\cdot\vec B=AB\cos\theta;\ |\vec A\times\vec B|=AB\sin\theta=\text{area};\ \text{projection}=\dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{B}\)
Step 1: \(\vec A\cdot\vec B=2-2+4=4;\ A=B=3\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\tfrac49\)
Step 2: \(\vec A\times\vec B=\hat i(4+2)-\hat j(2-4)+\hat k(-1-4)=6\hat i+2\hat j-5\hat k\)
Step 3: \(|\vec A\times\vec B|=\sqrt{36+4+25}=\sqrt{65};\ \text{projection}=\tfrac43\)
Worked derivation: \[\vec A\times\vec B=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&2&2\\2&-1&2\end{vmatrix}=6\hat i+2\hat j-5\hat k\]
Check: \[(\vec A\cdot\vec B)^2+|\vec A\times\vec B|^2=16+65=81=A^2B^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the dot product measures how much the vectors align and the cross product how much they are perpendicular, and together they recover }A^2B^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{dot product doubled; cross-product signs wrong}\); (B) \(\text{area is the magnitude }\sqrt{65};\ \text{sign of }\hat i\text{ wrong}\); (D) \(\text{vectors are not perpendicular}\).
Key point: \((\vec A\cdot\vec B)^2+|\vec A\times\vec B|^2=A^2B^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the impulse and average force when a ball is struck back along its line of approach, and the impulse from the area under a force–time graph
questions.question: A \(0.15\text{ kg}\) ball approaching at \(20\text{ m s}^{-1}\) is hit straight back at \(30\text{ m s}^{-1}\); contact lasts \(0.010\text{ s}\). In another case, a force rises linearly from 0 to \(600\text{ N}\) in \(0.01\text{ s}\) and falls linearly to 0 in the next \(0.01\text{ s}\). What are the impulse and average force in the first case and the impulse in the second?
options: A) \(7.5\text{ N s};\ 750\text{ N};\ 6.0\text{ N s}\)
B) \(1.5\text{ N s};\ 150\text{ N};\ 12\text{ N s}\)
C) \(7.5\text{ N s};\ 75\text{ N};\ 3.0\text{ N s}\)
D) \(4.5\text{ N s};\ 450\text{ N};\ 6.0\text{ N s}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(J=7.5\text{ N s},\ F_{\text{av}}=750\text{ N};\ J_2=6.0\text{ N s}\)
Given: \(m=0.15\text{ kg},\ u=-20,\ v=+30\text{ m s}^{-1},\ \Delta t=0.010\text{ s};\ \text{triangular }F(t),\ F_{\max}=600\text{ N},\ \text{base }0.02\text{ s}\)
Formula/Principle: \(J=\Delta p=m(v-u)=F_{\text{av}}\Delta t;\ J=\int F\,dt=\text{area under }F\text{–}t\)
Step 1: \(\Delta p=0.15(30-(-20))=0.15\times50=7.5\text{ N s}\)
Step 2: \(F_{\text{av}}=\dfrac{7.5}{0.010}=750\text{ N}\)
Step 3: \(J_2=\tfrac12\times0.02\times600=6.0\text{ N s}\)
Worked derivation: \[J=\int_0^{0.02}F\,dt=\frac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}=\frac12(0.02)(600)=6.0\ \text{N s}\]
Check: \[\text{velocity reverses, so speeds add: }20+30=50\ \text{m s}^{-1}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{momentum is a vector, so reversing direction makes the change the sum of the two speeds times mass}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{used }30-20;\ \text{triangle area not halved}\); (C) \(\text{average force divided wrongly}\); (D) \(\text{used only }30\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Key point: \(\Delta p=m(v-u)\text{ with signs};\ J=\text{area under }F\text{–}t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the work–energy theorem to identify which forces do work and how kinetic energy changes in sliding, circular and braking motion
questions.question: Which statement based on the work–energy theorem is correct?
options: A) The normal force on a block sliding on a horizontal floor does positive work
B) A centripetal force does work that increases the speed of a body in uniform circular motion

C) The net work done by all forces on a body equals its change in kinetic energy; for a block sliding on a rough horizontal floor, friction does negative work and the normal force and gravity do none, so the block slows; in uniform circular motion the centripetal force is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work, so the kinetic energy stays constant; for the same braking force, the stopping distance \(d=\dfrac{mu^2}{2F}\) quadruples when the initial speed doubles
D) The stopping distance doubles when the initial speed doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(W_{\text{net}}=\Delta K;\ \text{friction negative};\ \text{centripetal zero};\ d\propto u^2\)
Given: \(\text{sliding block, uniform circular motion, braking with constant force }F\)
Formula/Principle: \(W_{\text{net}}=K_f-K_i;\ W=\vec F\cdot\vec d=Fd\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(\text{normal force and gravity are perpendicular to horizontal motion}\Rightarrow W=0\)
Step 2: \(\text{friction opposite to displacement}\Rightarrow W<0\Rightarrow K\text{ decreases}\)
Step 3: \(-Fd=0-\tfrac12mu^2\Rightarrow d=\dfrac{mu^2}{2F}\propto u^2\)
Worked derivation: \[W_{\text{brake}}=-Fd=\Delta K=-\frac12mu^2\Rightarrow d=\frac{mu^2}{2F};\ u\to2u\Rightarrow d\to4d\]
Check: \[\text{circular motion: }\vec F_c\cdot\vec v=0\Rightarrow\frac{dK}{dt}=0\Rightarrow\text{speed constant}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only the component of force along the displacement does work, so perpendicular forces cannot change kinetic energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{normal force is perpendicular to the motion}\); (B) \(\text{centripetal force does no work}\); (D) \(d\propto u^2,\ \text{so it quadruples}\).
Key point: \(W_{\text{net}}=\Delta K;\ \text{perpendicular forces do no work}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Finding support reactions of a loaded beam using the conditions for rotational equilibrium, and the linear graph of one reaction against the load position
questions.question: A uniform 1.0 m beam weighing \(20\text{ N}\) rests on supports at its ends A and B. A \(40\text{ N}\) load is placed at distance \(x\) from A. Find the reactions when \(x=0.30\text{ m}\), and the equation of the graph of \(R_B\) against \(x\).
options: A) \(R_A=22\text{ N},\ R_B=38\text{ N};\ R_B=40x\)
B) \(R_A=30\text{ N},\ R_B=30\text{ N};\ R_B=30\text{ (constant)}\)
D) \(R_A=38\text{ N},\ R_B=22\text{ N};\ R_B=10+40x,\ \text{a straight line from }10\text{ N at }x=0\text{ to }50\text{ N at }x=1\text{ m}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(R_A=38\text{ N},\ R_B=22\text{ N};\ R_B=10+40x\)
Given: \(W=20\text{ N at }0.5\text{ m},\ L=40\text{ N at }x,\ \text{supports at }0\text{ and }1.0\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sum F=0,\ \sum\tau=0\ \text{about any point}\)
Step 1: \(R_A+R_B=60\text{ N}\)
Step 2: \(\tau\text{ about A: }R_B(1.0)=20(0.5)+40x\Rightarrow R_B=10+40x\)
Step 3: \(x=0.30:\ R_B=22\text{ N},\ R_A=38\text{ N}\)
Worked derivation: \[\tau_B:\ R_A(1.0)=20(0.5)+40(1-x)=50-40x\Rightarrow R_A+R_B=60\ \text{N}\]
Check: \[x=0.30:\ R_A=50-12=38\ \text{N},\ R_B=22\ \text{N},\ \text{sum }60\ \text{N}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the load is nearer A, so A carries the larger share; moving it towards B shifts the share linearly}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{reactions swapped; beam's own weight omitted}\); (B) \(\text{load position matters}\); (C) \(\text{beam weight's moment taken at the far end}\).
Key point: \(\text{take moments about one support to find the other reaction}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Scaling orbital period with orbit radius by Kepler's third law and comparing speeds at perihelion and aphelion from the law of areas
questions.question: A planet orbits the Sun at 4 times Earth's mean orbital radius. A comet's perihelion and aphelion distances are \(0.5\text{ AU}\) and \(4.5\text{ AU}\). What is the planet's period, the ratio of the comet's speeds at perihelion and aphelion, and which law gives that ratio?
options: A) \(4\text{ years};\ 1:1;\ \text{law of orbits}\)
B) \(8\text{ years};\ 9:1;\ \text{law of areas (angular momentum conserved, }v_pr_p=v_ar_a)\)
C) \(16\text{ years};\ 1:9;\ \text{law of periods}\)
D) \(2\text{ years};\ 3:1;\ \text{law of areas}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(8\text{ years};\ v_p:v_a=9:1;\ \text{law of areas}\)
Given: \(r=4r_E;\ r_p=0.5\text{ AU},\ r_a=4.5\text{ AU}\)
Formula/Principle: \(T^2\propto r^3;\ \dfrac{dA}{dt}=\dfrac{L}{2m}=\text{constant}\Rightarrow v_pr_p=v_ar_a\)
Step 1: \(T=T_E\left(\dfrac{r}{r_E}\right)^{3/2}=1\times4^{3/2}=8\text{ years}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{v_p}{v_a}=\dfrac{r_a}{r_p}=\dfrac{4.5}{0.5}=9\)
Step 3: \(\text{equal areas in equal times}\Rightarrow\text{fastest at perihelion}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{T^2}{T_E^2}=\frac{r^3}{r_E^3}=64\Rightarrow T=8\ \text{years}\]
Check: \[\text{comet: }a=\frac{0.5+4.5}{2}=2.5\ \text{AU}\Rightarrow T=2.5^{3/2}\approx4.0\ \text{years, consistent with }T^2\propto a^3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{gravity is central, so it exerts no torque about the Sun and angular momentum is conserved}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(T\propto r^{3/2},\ \text{not }r\); (C) \(\text{used }r^2\text{ and inverted ratio}\); (D) \(\text{used }\sqrt r\text{ and }\sqrt{9}\).
Key point: \(T\propto r^{3/2};\ v_pr_p=v_ar_a\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of vessels of different shapes, absolute pressure at depth in water, and the heights of mercury and water barometers
questions.question: Three vessels of different shapes are filled with water to the same height \(h\). Find the absolute pressure at \(10\text{ m}\) depth in water (\(P_a=1.01\times10^5\text{ Pa}\), \(\rho=1000\text{ kg m}^{-3}\), \(g=9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)) and the height of a water barometer when a mercury barometer (\(\rho_{Hg}=13.6\times10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}\)) reads \(76\text{ cm}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(\text{The widest vessel has the greatest bottom pressure};\ 0.98\times10^5\text{ Pa};\ 76\text{ cm}\)
B) \(\text{The narrowest vessel has the greatest bottom pressure};\ 1.01\times10^5\text{ Pa};\ 5.6\text{ cm}\)
C) \(\text{All three have equal bottom pressure }P_a+\rho gh\ (\text{hydrostatic paradox});\ 1.99\times10^5\text{ Pa}\approx2\text{ atm};\ 0.76\times13.6\approx10.3\text{ m}\)
D) \(\text{Bottom pressure depends on the volume of water};\ 2.0\times10^6\text{ Pa};\ 1.03\text{ m}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\text{equal pressures};\ 1.99\times10^5\text{ Pa};\ \approx10.3\text{ m}\)
Given: \(h=10\text{ m},\ \rho=1000,\ g=9.8;\ h_{Hg}=0.76\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=P_a+\rho gh;\ \rho_wh_w=\rho_{Hg}h_{Hg}\)
Step 1: \(\text{pressure depends only on depth, not on shape or volume}\)
Step 2: \(P=1.01\times10^5+1000\times9.8\times10=1.99\times10^5\text{ Pa}\)
Step 3: \(h_w=\dfrac{13.6\times10^3\times0.76}{1000}=10.3\text{ m}\)
Worked derivation: \[\rho_{Hg}gh_{Hg}=\rho_wgh_w\Rightarrow h_w=\frac{\rho_{Hg}}{\rho_w}h_{Hg}=13.6\times0.76=10.34\ \text{m}\]
Check: \[\rho gh=1000\times9.8\times10=0.98\times10^5\ \text{Pa}\approx1\ \text{atm extra}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the pressure at a point balances the weight of the column directly above it; the walls support any extra water}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{shape irrelevant; gauge pressure taken as absolute}\); (B) \(\text{shape irrelevant; water column is taller, not shorter}\); (D) \(\text{volume irrelevant; arithmetic wrong}\).
Key point: \(P=P_a+\rho gh\text{ depends only on depth}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating linear expansion of a heated rod, relating linear, area and volume expansion coefficients, and the thermal stress in a rod prevented from expanding
questions.question: A steel rod (\(\alpha=1.2\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}\), \(Y=2.0\times10^{11}\text{ Pa}\)) of length \(1.0\text{ m}\) is heated by \(50\text{ K}\). Find its expansion, the coefficients of area and volume expansion, and the stress if the rod is clamped rigidly at both ends. What happens to a hole in a heated steel plate?
options: A) \(0.60\text{ mm};\ 2.4\times10^{-5},\ 3.6\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1};\ 1.2\times10^8\text{ Pa};\ \text{the hole becomes larger}\)
B) \(6.0\text{ mm};\ 1.2\times10^{-5}\text{ each};\ 1.2\times10^{6}\text{ Pa};\ \text{the hole shrinks}\)
C) \(0.06\text{ mm};\ 3.6\times10^{-5},\ 2.4\times10^{-5};\ 0;\ \text{the hole is unchanged}\)
D) \(0.60\text{ mm};\ 1.44\times10^{-10},\ 1.73\times10^{-15};\ 2.4\times10^{8}\text{ Pa};\ \text{the hole shrinks}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\Delta L=0.60\text{ mm};\ \beta=2\alpha,\ \gamma=3\alpha;\ \sigma=1.2\times10^8\text{ Pa};\ \text{hole enlarges}\)
Given: \(L=1.0\text{ m},\ \alpha=1.2\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1},\ \Delta T=50\text{ K},\ Y=2.0\times10^{11}\text{ Pa}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta L=\alpha L\Delta T;\ \beta\approx2\alpha,\ \gamma\approx3\alpha;\ \sigma=Y\cdot\text{strain}=Y\alpha\Delta T\)
Step 1: \(\Delta L=1.2\times10^{-5}\times1.0\times50=6.0\times10^{-4}\text{ m}=0.60\text{ mm}\)
Step 2: \(\beta=2.4\times10^{-5},\ \gamma=3.6\times10^{-5}\ \text{K}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(\sigma=2.0\times10^{11}\times6.0\times10^{-4}=1.2\times10^8\text{ Pa}\)
Worked derivation: \[V=L^3\Rightarrow\Delta V=3L^2\Delta L=3L^3\alpha\Delta T\Rightarrow\gamma=\frac{\Delta V}{V\Delta T}=3\alpha\]
Check: \[\text{strain}=\frac{\Delta L}{L}=6.0\times10^{-4};\ \ \sigma=Y\times\text{strain}=1.2\times10^8\ \text{Pa}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a clamped rod is compressed back by exactly the amount it would have expanded, and every linear dimension of the plate, including the hole, scales up together}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{expansion ten times too large; }\beta,\gamma\text{ differ from }\alpha\); (C) \(\text{values swapped; clamping produces stress}\); (D) \(\text{coefficients add, not multiply}\).
Key point: \(\Delta L=\alpha L\Delta T;\ \gamma=3\alpha;\ \sigma=Y\alpha\Delta T\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the first law of thermodynamics to isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric, free-expansion and cyclic processes of an ideal gas
questions.question: Which statement about the first law \(\Delta U=Q-W\) (\(W\) = work done by the gas) is correct?
options: A) In an adiabatic expansion the gas absorbs heat, so its temperature rises
B) In an isochoric process all heat supplied is converted into work
C) In free expansion into a vacuum, the temperature of an ideal gas falls because it does work

D) In an isothermal process of an ideal gas \(\Delta U=0\), so \(Q=W\); in an adiabatic expansion \(Q=0\), so \(\Delta U=-W<0\) and the gas cools; in an isochoric process \(W=0\), so \(Q=\Delta U\); in free expansion \(Q=0\) and \(W=0\), so \(\Delta U=0\) and an ideal gas's temperature is unchanged; in a cyclic process \(\Delta U=0\), so the net heat absorbed equals the net work done
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\text{isothermal }Q=W;\ \text{adiabatic }\Delta U=-W;\ \text{isochoric }Q=\Delta U;\ \text{free expansion }\Delta U=0;\ \text{cycle }Q_{\text{net}}=W_{\text{net}}\)
Given: \(\text{ideal gas; }U\text{ depends only on }T\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta U=Q-W,\ W=\int P\,dV,\ \Delta U=nC_V\Delta T\)
Step 1: \(\text{isothermal: }\Delta T=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=0\Rightarrow Q=W\)
Step 2: \(\text{adiabatic: }Q=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=-W;\ \text{expansion }W>0\Rightarrow T\text{ falls}\)
Step 3: \(\text{isochoric: }dV=0\Rightarrow W=0;\ \text{free expansion: }P_{\text{ext}}=0,\ Q=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{cycle: }\oint dU=0\Rightarrow Q_{\text{net}}=W_{\text{net}}=\text{area enclosed on the }P\text{–}V\text{ diagram}\]
Check: \[\text{free expansion: }W=P_{\text{ext}}\Delta V=0\times\Delta V=0,\ Q=0\Rightarrow\Delta T=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so each constraint fixes one term and the first law gives the rest}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{adiabatic means }Q=0;\ \text{the gas cools on expansion}\); (B) \(\text{no work at constant volume}\); (C) \(\text{no work is done against a vacuum}\).
Key point: \(\Delta U=Q-W;\ \text{ideal gas: }U=U(T)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating rms speed and mean kinetic energy of gas molecules from kinetic theory, the temperature that doubles the rms speed, and the ratio of rms speeds of two gases
questions.question: For nitrogen (\(M=0.028\text{ kg mol}^{-1}\)) at \(300\text{ K}\), find the rms speed, the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule, the temperature at which the rms speed doubles, and the ratio of rms speeds of \(\text{O}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\) at the same temperature. questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(v_{\text{rms}}\approx517\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \bar K=6.21\times10^{-21}\text{ J};\ 1200\text{ K};\ 1:4\)
Given: \(M=0.028\text{ kg mol}^{-1},\ T=300\text{ K}\)
Formula/Principle: \(P=\tfrac13\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2\Rightarrow v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}};\ \bar K=\tfrac32k_BT\)
Step 1: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3\times8.314\times300}{0.028}}=\sqrt{2.67\times10^5}\approx517\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(\bar K=1.5\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times300=6.21\times10^{-21}\text{ J}\)
Step 3: \(v\propto\sqrt T\Rightarrow T\times4=1200\text{ K};\ \dfrac{v_{O_2}}{v_{H_2}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{32}}=\dfrac14\)
Worked derivation: \[PV=\frac13Nmv_{\text{rms}}^2=nRT\Rightarrow v_{\text{rms}}^2=\frac{3nRT}{Nm}=\frac{3RT}{M}\]
Check: \[\frac12mv_{\text{rms}}^2=\frac12\cdot\frac{0.028}{6.02\times10^{23}}\cdot2.67\times10^5\approx6.2\times10^{-21}\ \text{J}=\tfrac32k_BT\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{temperature measures mean kinetic energy, so at equal }T\text{ lighter molecules move faster}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{factor 3 omitted; }v\propto\sqrt T\text{ needs }4T\); (C) \(\text{doubling }T\text{ raises }v\text{ by }\sqrt2\text{ only; ratio is }1:4\); (D) \(\text{used }M\text{ in g mol}^{-1}\text{ wrongly}\).
Key point: \(v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{3RT/M};\ \bar K=\tfrac32k_BT\)
